CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5 · 29 HELPER LESSONS

Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Meet the people who keep our neighborhood running.

Every helper in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: look at the picture together, learn what the job really is, say the parent script, ask the questions, play the practice game and finish with a small understanding check. One helper a day is plenty — the whole class is a month of five-minute sessions, in whatever order your child’s curiosity points.

Start with the helpers your child already meets — doctor, bus driver, teacher — then follow the given order for the full journey: health helpers, safety helpers, learning helpers, food and growing helpers, and the people who build and fix everything else.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Doctor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson shows your child what doctors actually do, what their tools are for, and how a check-up works — so the real thing feels known instead of scary.

What is this?

A doctor is a body helper. When someone is sick or hurt, the doctor checks, finds out why, and treats it.

What does it mean?

Doctors work in clinics, hospitals and health vans. Their tools each have a job: a stethoscope listens to heartbeats, a small torch lights up ears and throats, a bandage protects a healing cut.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to know three things: doctors help bodies get better; a check-up is looking and listening, one small step at a time; and telling a grown-up where it hurts is the fastest way to get help.

Why this matters

Doctor play and doctor talk give your child the words and the script for real appointments. A known story is a calmer story — for both of you.

What it teaches

Vocabulary (doctor, patient, stethoscope, check-up), body awareness, asking-for-help skills, and trust in helpers — plus sequenced thinking as your child retells the visit in order.

Words to learn

doctorpatientstethoscopecheck-uphealthymedicine

Say this to your child

“"When something hurts, you tell me and we visit the doctor. The doctor looks and listens very carefully, and then your body gets a plan to get better. You can always tell the doctor how it feels."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a doctor. Doctors help our bodies when we are sick or hurt."
  2. Point to the picture: find the stethoscope, the coat, the kind face. Ask what each might be for.
  3. Explain the visit in order: we say what hurts, the doctor looks and listens, then we get a plan to feel better.
  4. Be honest: some checks feel odd — a cold stethoscope, a puff of air, a look up your nose. Saying how it feels to the doctor is always allowed.
  5. Practise the visit end to end in pretend play before any real appointment.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child to find: what is on the doctor’s head or neck? What is in the doctor’s hands? Where do you think the doctor is working? Who is the doctor helping?

Ask your child

"What does a doctor do all day?" "Which tool listens to your heart?" "What could you tell the doctor if your tummy hurt?" "How could we make a check-up feel easier?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The doctor helps me get better," "The stethoscope goes thump-thump on my chest," or practise the brave sentence: "My knee hurts here."

Out in the real world

Point out doctor things in daily life: the clinic you pass, the nurse at preschool, the first-aid box at the pool, medicine with a "grown-ups only" label at the pharmacy.

Try it together

Teddy clinic: your child is the doctor. Listen to Ted’s heart with a cardboard-tube stethoscope, look in his ears with a torch (off), wrap a tissue bandage, and say kindly: "Tell me where it hurts." Swap roles so your child is the patient too — that is the bravery rehearsal.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who do you tell when something hurts? What does the doctor listen with? What could you say to the doctor at your check-up?" Three answers = lesson landed.

Parent tips

Never use the doctor as a threat or a punishment — it turns a helper into a bogeyman. Read a doctor-visit book the day before appointments, let your child pack a toy, and afterwards name the brave moments out loud.

Staying safe

Medicine is only given by grown-ups — never take pills or syrup like sweets, even when it smells nice. Sharp things at the clinic are the doctor’s tools only.

This lesson pairs with the Doctor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

What happens at the doctor? Take a gentle visit: the Doctor Visit class walks a whole check-up in order — appointment to goodbye — with a teddy bear on every step.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Nurse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches who nurses are, what they do all day beside doctors, and gives your child a caring job to practise at home.

What is this?

A nurse is a caring helper who looks after sick and hurt people — checking them, comforting them and explaining everything.

What does it mean?

Nurses work in hospitals, clinics, schools and vaccination vans. They measure temperature, wrap bandages, give the medicine doctors prescribe, and teach families how to keep healing at home.

What does the child need to know?

Nurses stay with patients the longest — they are the ones who explain, comfort and check again. When your child knows the nurse by role, check-ups gain a familiar friendly face.

Why this matters

Nursing is visible kindness: calm voice, gentle hands, careful checking. Children absorb that caring is something people DO — and copy it on dolls, siblings and pets.

What it teaches

Empathy, gentle-touch control, sequencing (check → comfort → explain), health vocabulary, and the confidence to ask "what are you doing now?" during real care.

Words to learn

nursepatientthermometerbandagecomfortgentle

Say this to your child

“"Nurses help the doctor take care of you. They check how you are, they make hurts feel better, and they explain every single thing they do. Nurses have gentle hands and kind voices."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a nurse. Nurses take care of people — with the doctor and on their own."
  2. Point out the picture: what is the nurse holding? What is on the walls? Who is being cared for?
  3. Walk the nurse’s day: check temperature → wrap the arm → explain each step → smile. Act it with your hands as you say it.
  4. Teach the caring script: "I am going to check you now, all right? Tell me if it feels strange."
  5. Practise on a patient who cannot talk — a teddy — so all attention goes to the gentle hands.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the nurse doing first? What is on the tray or in the pockets? Can you find a smile — on the nurse or the patient? What tells you this nurse is being careful?

Ask your child

"What does a nurse check first?" "What would you say before you wrap a teddy’s paw?" "Who takes care of you when you are poorly?" "How can our hands be nurse-hands?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the caring lines out loud: "I will check you now — tell me if it feels strange," "All wrapped up, all better," and the asking line: "What are you doing now?"

Out in the real world

Nurses are everywhere once you look: the school first-aid drawer, the clinic waiting room, the vaccination nurse, bandage boxes at home. Each spotting moment is a mini-recap.

Try it together

Caring corner: one blanket "bed", one doll or teddy, toilet-paper bandages, a paper "thermometer". Your child is the nurse — check, wrap, explain, comfort. Ten minutes of this is a whole social-emotional lesson.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who checks people beside the doctor? What do nurses wrap hurts with? Show me your gentle nurse hands." The hands will tell you everything.

Parent tips

Praise the caring behaviours you see ("you checked Ted so gently") — nurse talk makes gentleness cool. If a real check-up is coming, tell your child the nurse will explain first; knowing that halves the wobbles.

Staying safe

Bandage play is pretend — real hurts need a grown-up’s eyes first. Medicine, even "just once more", is a grown-up job only.

This lesson pairs with the Nurse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Paramedic — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns siren panic into understanding: who is inside the ambulance, what they carry, and what your family does in a real emergency.

What is this?

A paramedic is a fast health helper. In a big emergency, they come quickly in an ambulance to help the person and take them to hospital.

What does it mean?

An ambulance is a rescue car with lights, a siren and a mini-hospital inside: stretchers, oxygen, bandages, a radio. Paramedics check the patient on the spot and keep helping all the ride to hospital.

What does the child need to know?

Three things your child should carry home: the siren means help is on the way, the emergency number (practise yours), and in an emergency we find a grown-up — fast and loudly.

Why this matters

Emergencies are frightening because they are unknown. Naming the helpers, the vehicle and the family plan gives your child a script — and scripts shrink fear.

What it teaches

Emergency vocabulary, number memory, listening under stress (practised calmly!), community-trust building, and sequencing: call → helpers arrive → check → hospital.

Words to learn

paramedicambulanceemergencysirenstretcherfirst aid

Say this to your child

“"If something bad happens, we tell a grown-up right away — loud and clear. Grown-ups call the emergency number, and the paramedics come fast with their ambulance to help."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a paramedic. When there is a big emergency, paramedics come fast to help."
  2. Find the ambulance parts: lights, siren, the cross, the wheels that go very fast.
  3. Explain the noise honestly: "The siren is loud so cars hear it and move — that is how help gets there quickly."
  4. Learn your family emergency number today: say it, tap it on a toy phone, sing it. Three tiny rehearsals beat one big lecture.
  5. Rehearse the family rule: big trouble → shout for a grown-up → grown-up calls. Never play-call emergencies for fun.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is on top of the ambulance? What colours do you see? What is the paramedic holding? Where do you think the patient rides — can you find the windows?

Ask your child

"Who comes in an ambulance?" "Why is the siren so loud?" "What would you do if someone fell and could not get up?" "What is our emergency number?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the shout: "Grown-up, come quick, help please!" and the number, spoken clearly twice. Then the calm sentence: "The paramedics are coming to help."

Out in the real world

When a siren passes, stop and listen: "Someone needs help — and helpers are coming." Ambulance open days let children sit inside; the radio alone is worth the trip.

Try it together

Teddy rescue: Ted "falls" off the sofa. Your child shouts for a grown-up (you), you "call", the toy ambulance rushes over, paramedic checks Ted on a shoebox stretcher, everyone recovers. Repeat weekly — rehearsal is the point.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who comes to help in a big emergency? What do we do first? Say our emergency number." Loud-and-clear shout + number = pass.

Parent tips

Sensitive children may need the siren named BEFORE it happens. Keep the number learning light — songs and toy phones, never quizzes. Praise every "I told a grown-up", real or pretend.

Staying safe

Emergency numbers are for real emergencies only — never for fun calls. Ambulance bays and moving trucks are out of bounds; children watch from far back with a grown-up.

This lesson pairs with the Paramedic flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Police Officer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces police officers as neighborhood helpers and reheases the one plan every child should own: what to do if you ever get lost.

What is this?

A police officer is a safety helper for everyone in the neighborhood — the person to find when someone is lost, scared or in trouble.

What does it mean?

Officers patrol on foot, on bikes and in marked cars. They help lost children, stop dangerous driving, sort out arguments and find out what happened after accidents. A badge and a radio are their tools.

What does the child need to know?

Two messages, in balance: officers are helpers we can trust — AND in any worry, our first job is to find a grown-up we know. Practise both; they work together.

Why this matters

"Find the badge" is a concrete, findable plan for a small person in a big scary moment. Concrete beats abstract at four.

What it teaches

Community trust, safety scripting, self-talk under stress ("I am lost, I will find a helper"), plus personal-information memory: your name, your grown-up’s name, your street.

Words to learn

police officerbadgesafelosttrustradio

Say this to your child

“"Police officers are helpers. If we are ever lost, we stay where we are and ask a grown-up with a badge: ‘I am lost — my grown-up is…’ And we always tell someone we trust, too."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a police officer. Officers keep our neighborhood safe and help anyone in trouble."
  2. Find the badge and the radio. "The badge tells everyone: this is a helper. The radio talks to other helpers."
  3. Tell one helping story concretely: an officer found a lost child and walked them back to their grown-up.
  4. Learn the get-found plan today: stay where you are → look for a grown-up with a badge or a parent with children → say "I am lost" + your grown-up’s name.
  5. Rehearse it as a game with teddies — then quietly again next week.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: can you find the badge? The radio? What is the officer wearing? Does the officer look kind? What might the officer be looking at?

Ask your child

"Who do officers help?" "What would you say if you were lost?" "What does the badge mean?" "Who are the grown-ups YOU trust?"

What your child can say or do

The key sentence, spoken twice, loud and clear: "I am lost — please help me find my grown-up." Plus your family’s grown-up name and street, practised until easy.

Out in the real world

Wave to officers you pass; visit a station open day. Toy police cars in the bath become helping stories when you narrate who they rescue.

Try it together

Teddy is lost in the "shop" (another room). Your child the officer finds him, kneels down, and teddy practises the sentence. Swap: your child is lost, you are the officer. Repetition is the safety net.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a police officer do? What would you say if you were lost? What is my first name?" Clear sentence + your name = lesson landed.

Parent tips

Keep it warm, never scary: officers are helpers, not monsters and not magicians. Balance matters — "we look for a known grown-up first, and a badge is a good find". Avoid threat-based policing talk entirely.

Staying safe

Rehearse calmly, never with threats. Agree the family rule together and repeat it on every busy-street outing: stay put, find a helper, say the sentence.

This lesson pairs with the Police Officer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Firefighter — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson covers what firefighters do — fighting fires AND preventing them — and walks your family through the one drill that matters.

What is this?

A firefighter is an emergency helper who puts out fires, rescues people and pets, and teaches everyone how to stop fires from starting.

What does it mean?

Firefighters ride a big red truck with ladders, hoses and water. Their gear — helmet, heavy coat, gloves, an air mask — protects them inside smoke and heat.

What does the child need to know?

The three fire rules for small people: matches and lighters are grown-up tools (tell a grown-up if you find one); smoke means get low, get out, stay out; firefighters in masks are helpers, even when they look and sound strange.

Why this matters

Fire is the scariest "what if" of early childhood — and the most fixable. A drilled plan plus mask-familiarity changes outcomes; this is the highest-value safety lesson in the whole class.

What it teaches

Safety scripting, family teamwork, sequencing (alarm → low → out → meeting spot), mask-and-noise desensitisation, and the prevention mindset: firefighters stop fires before they start.

Words to learn

firefightersmokehelmetescapemeeting spotemergency

Say this to your child

“"If there is ever smoke or fire, we do not hide — we get low, we get outside, and we stay outside at our meeting spot. The firefighters come to help us. We never go back inside, not even for a toy."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a firefighter. Firefighters put out fires and rescue people."
  2. Find the gear: helmet, coat, boots. "The suit is thick and the mask looks funny — but it is a helper suit. It keeps the firefighter safe inside smoke."
  3. Talk prevention first: "Most firefighter work is stopping fires before they happen. Matches? Grown-up tools. Candle? Grown-up tool."
  4. Teach the escape script: hear the alarm → get low and crawl under the smoke → get outside → STAY out → meet at our family spot.
  5. Drill it as a game today: crawl between sofa cushions, count to the meeting spot, cheer. Repeat twice a year.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the firefighter wearing? Can you find the helmet — why is it hard? What colour is the truck behind? What does the firefighter carry?

Ask your child

"What do firefighters ride in?" "What do we do if we hear the smoke alarm?" "Are matches for children or grown-ups?" "Where is our family meeting spot?"

What your child can say or do

The escape line, shouted happily: "Get low, get out, stay out!" plus "Matches are grown-up tools — I will tell you!" And your address, spoken slowly once.

Out in the real world

Walk past the fire station and look at the truck doors. Point out smoke alarms at home and press-test them together so the sound is known, not feared.

Try it together

Fire-drill game: teddy "cooking" leaves a "fire" (red scarf). Alarm sounds (clap-clap), everyone crawls low to the door, out to the meeting spot (the hallway plant). Then — the firefighter puppet arrives to put it out. Repeat until boring; boring is the goal.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do when the alarm sounds? What do we do if we find matches? Where do we meet outside?" Three crisp answers = drill landed.

Parent tips

Masks scare children who have never seen one. Fire-station open days fix this permanently — the voice behind the mask is a person who loves dogs. Never use fire or firefighters as a threat.

Staying safe

This is the safety lesson: matches, lighters and candles are grown-up tools — always tell a grown-up. Real drill: low, out, stay out, never go back in. Do the drill, don’t just read it.

This lesson pairs with the Firefighter flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Crossing Guard — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the crossing guard’s job and drills the road-crossing routine your child will use every single day of childhood.

What is this?

A crossing guard is a road helper who stops traffic so children and families can cross the street safely.

What does it mean?

Crossing guards wear bright vests and carry a stop sign. They stand at busy crossings at school times, watch the cars, step out, hold up the sign, and wave people across when the way is clear.

What does the child need to know?

The routine: wait at the kerb, listen for the guard, cross only on the guard’s or your grown-up’s signal, and hold hands the whole way. Streets are for crossing, never for playing.

Why this matters

Roads are the most dangerous place in a child’s daily life. A drill with a rhythm — stop, look, listen, hold — is remembered by the body, not just the head.

What it teaches

Self-control at kerbs (the hardest skill!), left-right scanning, listening for engines, hand-holding cooperation, and traffic vocabulary.

Words to learn

crossing guardkerbtrafficstop signsafecross

Say this to your child

“"At the kerb we stop. We look left, look right, look left again. We listen for cars. Then we hold my hand and cross together — and we never run."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a crossing guard. They stop the cars so we can cross safely."
  2. Find the stop sign and the bright vest. "Cars can see the bright colours from far away."
  3. Teach the four beats with hand motions: STOP (hand flat), LOOK (hand over eyes), LISTEN (hand to ear), HOLD (squeeze hands).
  4. Practise the beats at a pretend kerb — a rug edge — with teddies as traffic.
  5. Then do it for real on your next walk, narrating quietly: "Stop… look… listen… now we hold hands and cross."

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the guard holding up? What colours can you find on the vest? Which way is the guard looking? Where are the children standing — on the road or at the kerb?

Ask your child

"What does the stop sign tell the cars?" "What do we do first at the kerb?" "Why do we hold hands?" "Can we play on the road?"

What your child can say or do

The four beats, chanted: "Stop, look, listen, hold!" And the rule, in their own words: "We cross with a grown-up, never alone."

Out in the real world

Greet your real crossing guard by role — "there is the crossing guard keeping us safe" — and let your child wave. The routine becomes a relationship, and relationships stick.

Try it together

Cushion kerb: line up cushions as the road, teddies drive toy cars, your child is the guard with a paper stop sign. They must hold the sign, count "one, two, three, safe!", then wave the teddies across. Swap roles.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do first at the kerb? Who stops the cars? Do we run or walk?" Stop + guard + walking = pass.

Parent tips

Never step into the road with a moving car "to show what happens" — the drill is always done safe. Reward the wait: patience at the kerb is the win, not speed.

Staying safe

Never cross alone, never run across, never play near roads — even quiet ones. Cars need a long time to stop; small children are hard for drivers to see.

This lesson pairs with the Crossing Guard flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Lifeguard — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the lifeguard’s watching job and sets the water rules your child will use at every pool, beach and bath.

What is this?

A lifeguard is a water-safety helper who watches everyone in the water and helps the moment something goes wrong.

What does it mean?

Lifeguards sit in a tall chair by pools or on beaches, watching all the time. They blow a whistle when something is unsafe, rescue people with a buoy or tube, and know first aid.

What does the child need to know?

Water rules for fours: we ask a grown-up before any water play; a lifeguard’s whistle means freeze and listen; we walk near water, never run; a grown-up is always in the water with non-swimmers.

Why this matters

Rules feel unfair until they have a person and a reason. The lifeguard — watching IS helping — makes pool rules make sense, which is exactly when children follow them.

What it teaches

Listening-and-freezing control (a genuine safety skill), rule reasoning, water vocabulary, and the asking-before-doing habit that generalises to every risky place.

Words to learn

lifeguardwhistlerescuedeepshallowwalk

Say this to your child

“"The lifeguard watches the water all the time. When we hear the whistle, we stop and listen. Near water we walk — and a grown-up is always with us."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a lifeguard. They watch the water and keep swimmers safe."
  2. Find the tall chair, the whistle, the rescue ring. "Sitting up high lets the lifeguard see EVERYONE."
  3. Give the whistle meaning: "One whistle means stop and look at the lifeguard. It is not scolding — it is helping."
  4. Teach the asking habit: any water — pool, bucket, bath, sea — gets a grown-up check first.
  5. Rehearse the freeze game at bath time so the listening reflex exists before a real pool day.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: where does the lifeguard sit — high or low? Why so high? What is the lifeguard holding? Can you find someone swimming? What colours say "safety" on this card?

Ask your child

"What does the lifeguard’s whistle mean?" "Why does the lifeguard sit so high?" "Do we run or walk near the pool?" "Who do we ask before we go in the water?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the freeze: you whistle softly, your child stops and looks. And the asking line: "May I go in the water?" — said before any water play.

Out in the real world

At the pool, find the lifeguard together: "See how they never stop watching? That is their whole job." Beach flags and pool-depth signs are lifeguard language — decode one.

Try it together

Bath lifeguard: your child is the lifeguard on the "chair" (closed toilet lid, towels for a tower). You wash a doll; lifeguard blows a pretend whistle; doll freezes; lifeguard says "safe!" Swap and let them run the whistle show.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the whistle mean? Walk or run at the pool? Who goes in the water with you?" Freeze + walk + grown-up = pass.

Parent tips

Never treat the whistle as punishment — it is a helper’s voice. Praise fast freezing; the speed IS the safety. If your child is swim-shy, the lifeguard can be introduced as "the person who helps everyone feel brave".

Staying safe

Never swim without a grown-up actually in the water. No running on wet pool sides. Ponds, buckets and paddling pools count as water — the asking rule covers them all.

This lesson pairs with the Lifeguard flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Teacher — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the classroom door: what teachers actually do, the little rules that make class work, and a rehearsal for your child’s own school days.

What is this?

A teacher is a learning helper who shows children new things — letters, numbers, songs, science, and how to be a good friend.

What does it mean?

Teachers work in schools. They plan the day, explain ideas step by step, read aloud, help with sharing and turn-taking, and tell families how the day went.

What does the child need to know?

Classroom know-how: teachers love questions, we raise a hand to take a turn, and "I need help" is a welcome sentence, not a failure.

Why this matters

A teacher is your child’s first grown-up outside the family. Knowing the job and the routines turns first-days wobble into "I know how this works".

What it teaches

School-readiness scripting, question-asking courage, listening turns, memory retell (what did we learn today?), and respect-for-guides that transfers to coaches and librarians.

Words to learn

teacherclassroomraise your handlearnquestionturn

Say this to your child

“"Teachers help us learn. When you wonder about something, raise your hand and ask — teachers LOVE questions. And if something is tricky, saying ‘help me please’ is exactly right."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a teacher. Teachers help children learn new things every day."
  2. Find the classroom things on the card: books, board, children listening. What is YOUR classroom like?
  3. Explain the rhythm of a school day: come in, listen, try, play, ask, go home. Use your hands to show the day’s shape.
  4. Teach the two golden moves: raise your hand to speak, and say "I need help" proudly.
  5. Rehearse with play-school so the moves feel familiar before they are needed.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the teacher holding or pointing at? What are the children doing — are they taking turns? What can you see on the walls? Does the classroom look calm or loud?

Ask your child

"What does a teacher do all day?" "What do we do when we want to say something in class?" "What could you ask your teacher tomorrow?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the two moves: "Can I say something?" (hand up) and "I need help, please." Both said proudly — needing help is a skill, not a shame.

Out in the real world

At home, teachers are everywhere: swimming coaches, library story readers, dance teachers. Name the role each time — "your coach is teaching like a teacher".

Try it together

Play-school: your child teaches teddies one song, one letter and one rule. Then swap — you are the student who raises a hand, asks a silly-good question and says "I need help". The swap is where the magic lands.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a teacher do? What do we do when we want to talk in class? What do we say when something is tricky?" Question + hand + help = pass.

Parent tips

Never joke "wait till real school!" — school should sound like a place with friendly helpers. Ask "what did your teacher show today?" at dinner; retelling builds memory and gives you a window.

This lesson pairs with the Teacher flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Librarian — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the library a known place before the first visit: who the librarian is, how borrowing works, and the little skills that make trips joyful.

What is this?

A librarian is a book helper who takes care of the library and helps every visitor find exactly the right book.

What does it mean?

Libraries hold thousands of books everyone can borrow for free. Librarians arrange them so they can be found, run story times, and lend books with a library card.

What does the child need to know?

Library skills: books live in order, we ask the librarian to find things, borrowing means take-home-and-bring-back, and the library voice is soft.

Why this matters

A library card is a child’s first membership of the grown-up world. Knowing the borrowing loop — choose, borrow, care, return — is responsibility with stories as the reward.

What it teaches

Sequencing (choose→borrow→read→return), care-of-shared-things, asking-adults-for-help, quiet-voice self-regulation, and print motivation — the strongest early-reading predictor.

Words to learn

librarianlibraryborrowreturnstory timecard

Say this to your child

“"The librarian helps us find wonderful books. We borrow them with our card, read them at home, and bring them back for the next family. Librarians know where every dinosaur hides."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a librarian. They help us find books and take them home."
  2. Find the shelves, the books, the helper. "There are so many books — the librarian knows where every one lives."
  3. Explain borrowing like a tick-tock: choose a book → the librarian stamps it → we take it home → we read it lots → we bring it back so the next child can love it.
  4. Practise the library voice: whisper "where are the truck books?" — then practise asking it, because librarians LOVE that question.
  5. Plan the first visit: what two books will you look for?

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the librarian doing — reading, helping, tidying? How many books can you count? What would YOU look for first on those shelves?

Ask your child

"Who helps us find books?" "What happens when we borrow a book?" "What do we do with a book we love and finished?" "What should we ask the librarian on our visit?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the ask: "Where are the books about trucks, please?" And the borrowing line at the counter: "I would like to borrow these books, please."

Out in the real world

Libraries run free story times — go once and your child meets the librarian in their favourite role. Spot "return here" boxes around town: book journeys never stop.

Try it together

Home library: line up ten books face-out, make paper "cards", take turns being librarian and borrower. The stamp can be a sticker; the return basket is the book-drop. Repeat until the loop is automatic.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who helps us in the library? What do we do with a borrowed book when we finish? Show me your library voice." Helper + return + whisper = pass.

Parent tips

Let your child carry the card and hand the books over — the transaction IS the lesson. Damaged-book moments happen; talk kindly about caring for borrowed things and move on.

This lesson pairs with the Librarian flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Mail Carrier — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson follows one letter’s journey and gives your child a real one to send — mail is the most concrete community helper magic there is.

What is this?

A mail carrier is a delivery helper who brings letters, cards and parcels to every home on the street — and carries our post away to the people we love.

What does it mean?

Mail carriers walk or drive a route with a big bag, sorted in address order. Letters travel from post box to sorting office to route — sometimes with a plane or train in between.

What does the child need to know?

The posting loop: write → envelope → stamp → post box → mail carrier → the right letterbox. And the golden rule: our letterbox and mail truck are the carrier’s workplace, not toys.

Why this matters

Posting real mail connects writing to love: your scribble becomes a grandparent’s smile. Address, stamp and delivery stop being abstract words and become a thing your child DID.

What it teaches

Sequencing across days (write today, arrive Thursday — patience!), address awareness, name-writing motivation, community maps, and giver’s joy.

Words to learn

mail carrierletterenvelopestamppost boxdeliver

Say this to your child

“"The mail carrier brings us letters and parcels, and takes ours away to the people we love. A drawing from your hands can travel across the whole town — or the whole world."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a mail carrier. They bring letters to our home and take ours away."
  2. Find the bag, the letters, the truck. "The bag is heavy — the letters inside are for many different houses!"
  3. Trace the journey with your finger: our table → post box → sorting office (the letters get sorted like socks!) → the mail carrier’s bag → Grandmother’s letterbox.
  4. Read an envelope together: name, street, town. "The address is the letter’s home address!"
  5. Make a real letter today — the lesson only lands when something is actually posted.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the mail carrier carrying? How many letterboxes can you count? What colour is the truck? Is it raining or sunny — do mail carriers still work?

Ask your child

"Who brings our letters? Where does our letter go after the post box? What is on the front of an envelope? Who could we send a picture to?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the send-off: "Dear Grandma, I made this for you!" — your child "writes" their name and tells you whose letter it is and where it is going.

Out in the real world

Walk to a real post box and post something real. Track bin-and-mail days on a family calendar; watch for the carrier on your street and wave.

Try it together

Home post office: shoebox counter, paper stamps, envelopes, a sock "mail bag". Family members write notes; your child sorts by person and delivers to letterboxes made of cereal boxes. Sorting = the real job.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who brings our mail? Where does a letter go after we post it? What do we put on the envelope?" Carrier + sorting + address = pass.

Parent tips

The waiting is the lesson: mark on the calendar when the letter should arrive. If the carrier comes, a wave and "thank you!" from the doorstep beats any worksheet.

Staying safe

Never open other people’s post or mailboxes, and never play behind a parked delivery van — drivers cannot see small people there.

This lesson pairs with the Mail Carrier flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bus Driver — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole bus experience — waiting, boarding, riding, ringing, exiting — so the first real ride belongs to your child.

What is this?

A bus driver is a travel helper who drives people around the neighborhood, stop by stop, safely.

What does it mean?

Buses run on fixed routes with marked stops. The driver steers, opens the doors, keeps everyone safe and follows the route plan. Passengers pay, sit and hold on.

What does the child need to know?

Bus know-how: wait at the stop, board after others leave, pay or tap, sit and hold, ring for your stop, wait for full stop before standing, and exit with a grown-up.

Why this matters

Public transport is a bundle of life skills in one ride: patience, money, seating, sequencing. And counting stops is real maths with motion.

What it teaches

Sequencing and waiting, money handling, stop counting (maths!), bell-pressing agency, and road-safety transfer: buses are big, drivers sit high, small people are hard to see.

Words to learn

bus driverbus stopfareroutestop bellboard

Say this to your child

“"The bus driver takes us safely to our stop. We wait for the bus to stop, pay our fare, sit down and hold on. When our stop comes, we ring the bell!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a bus driver. They take people where they need to go — stop by stop."
  2. Find the wheel, the doors, the seats. "The driver watches the road with big mirrors so everyone rides safely."
  3. Walk the ride sequence with your hands: stop → doors open → pay → sit and hold → ring → doors open → off.
  4. Practise the hold: sitting bottoms stay on seats, hands hold the rail, and we wait for the bus to stop fully before standing.
  5. Plan a real one-stop ride this week — one stop out, walk back, memory made.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: where does the driver sit? Can you find the doors? How many passengers can you count? What is outside the windows?

Ask your child

"Who drives the bus? What do we do when we get on? When can we stand up? What do we press before our stop?"

What your child can say or do

Practise the fare hand-over: "One ticket, please!" And the safety rule in their words: "I stay seated and hold on until the bus stops."

Out in the real world

Any bus ride becomes a lesson: count stops aloud, spot the driver’s mirrors, find the route map. Trams, trains and ferries all run the same script.

Try it together

Chair bus: line up chairs, punch tickets from scrap paper, call stops ("Next stop: Library!"), a spoon in a cup rings the bell. Everyone boards with teddies and pays with buttons.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do at the stop? When do we stand up? What do we press before our stop?" Wait + sit-till-stop + bell = pass.

Parent tips

Board after passengers get off; let your child drop coins in the fare box — the clink is their moment. Talk to the driver when boarding if the queue allows; "thank you, driver!" lands beautifully.

Staying safe

Stay seated and holding while the bus moves. Never walk directly behind a bus — the driver cannot see small people there. Always exit with a grown-up.

This lesson pairs with the Bus Driver flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Pilot — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson walks a flight from checklist to landing and turns airport overwhelm into a known story with your child as co-pilot.

What is this?

A pilot is a flying helper who flies aeroplanes, taking people and things safely across the sky.

What does it mean?

Pilots sit in the cockpit with screens, buttons and a steering wheel called a yoke. Before every flight they check the plane, plan the route and talk with the airport tower by radio.

What does the child need to know?

Flight know-how: pilots check everything BEFORE flying, the tower helps guide them, and at the airport children hold a grown-up’s hand and stay behind the lines.

Why this matters

Airports are sensory chaos for fours — belts, queues, loudspeakers. A pilot story gives the trip a hero and a script, and contrails turn every future sky-gaze into spotting helpers.

What it teaches

Sequencing (check→taxi→take-off→fly→land), big-map thinking (world is huge, planes cross it), radio-play dialogue, weather curiosity, and waiting skills at real airports.

Words to learn

pilotcockpittowertake offlandco-pilot

Say this to your child

“"The pilot checks everything, then flies the plane up above the clouds. The tower talks to the pilot on the radio the whole way. Before we take off, everyone buckles up — even teddies."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a pilot. Pilots fly aeroplanes and keep everyone on board safe."
  2. Find the cockpit, the windows, the wings. "The pilot sits at the very front — the best office window in the world!"
  3. Tell the flight in five beats: check the plane → taxi down the runway → take off → fly above the clouds → land. Act each with your arm.
  4. Explain the tower: "The people in the tower watch every plane and talk to pilots by radio — helper talking to helper."
  5. Play the whole flight before any real trip, so belts and take-off sounds are old friends.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the pilot wearing? What can you see through the cockpit windows? Where do the wings go? What might the pilot’s hands be doing?

Ask your child

"Who flies the plane? Who talks to the pilot on the radio? What happens right before take-off? What is above the clouds?"

What your child can say or do

The countdown: "Three, two, one — take off!" And the pre-flight line: "We check everything first." Plus the airport rule: "Hold a grown-up’s hand."

Out in the real world

Watch real contrails and wave. Airport trips: belts go in the tray, planes go up. Picture books about first flights read the night before work wonders.

Try it together

Chair plane: two chairs, seatbelts of dressing-gown belts, teddies stowed. Pilot announces: "Cabin ready? Check the wings!" Tower (you, holding a toy phone) clears take-off; everyone counts down; arms out; fly over the ocean rug; land softly at the sofa airport. Swap tower and pilot roles.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who flies the plane? Who talks to pilots on the radio? What do we do before take-off?" Pilot + tower + buckle-up = pass.

Parent tips

Loud take-off noises are less scary when named in advance: "The engines roar when we go fast — that is the plane getting strong." Let your child pack a plane bag: agency calms nerves.

Staying safe

At airports: hold hands, stay behind lines, belts and trays are for grown-ups to manage. Aeroplanes are flown by trained pilots — never by children, even very enthusiastic ones.

This lesson pairs with the Pilot flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Farmer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson follows food from soil to plate and hands your child a real farmer’s job: growing something from seed, day by day.

What is this?

A farmer is a food helper who grows vegetables, fruit and grains, and cares for farm animals.

What does it mean?

Farms have fields, greenhouses, barns and tractors. Farmers plant, water, weed, harvest, feed animals and carry the food to markets and shops for all of us.

What does the child need to know?

Food knowledge for fours: food grows in soil or on trees and plants, animals give us milk and eggs, and every carrot in the shop was grown by someone.

Why this matters

"Where does food come from?" is a four-year-old’s favourite mystery. Knowing the farmer grows brave eating — children try foods they helped imagine from seed.

What it teaches

Patience across days (the farmer’s core lesson), plant-life-cycle sequencing, responsibility routines (daily watering), nature vocabulary, and food-to-farm mapping.

Words to learn

farmerseedharvestcropsbarnsoil

Say this to your child

“"Farmers grow our food. A carrot starts as a tiny seed — the farmer waters it and waits, and waits, until one day it is ready. Farmers are patient helpers."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a farmer. Farmers grow the food we eat and take care of farm animals."
  2. Find the fields, the tractor, the animals. "The tractor helps the farmer work the big fields."
  3. Tell the seed story: seed into soil → rain and sun → roots drink → sprout → grow → harvest → shop → OUR plate. Use your arm as the growing stem.
  4. Match tonight’s dinner to farms: "This potato? A farmer dug it up. This apple? Picked from a tree."
  5. Start the windowsill farm today — the lesson is not finished until something sprouts.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the farmer holding? Which animals can you find? Where do you think the food goes after the farm? Is it planting time or harvest time on this card?

Ask your child

"Where do carrots come from?" "What does the farmer plant?" "Who gives us milk and eggs?" "What are YOU growing on our windowsill?"

What your child can say or do

The farmer’s patience line: "Seeds need water, sun and time." And the dinner recap: "The farmer grew this, the shop sold it, we cooked it!"

Out in the real world

Farmers’ markets let your child meet real growers — ask one question ("what is ripe now?"). Farm-visit days in autumn are worth the trip: pumpkins, tractors, mud.

Try it together

Windowsill farm: beans on wet cotton in a jar, or herb seeds in a cup. Your child is the farmer: water daily, check leaves, measure with a ribbon. First sprout = celebration; first wilt = farmer problem-solving.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who grows our food? What does a seed need to grow? What did the farmer harvest?" Food + water-sun-time + naming a crop = pass.

Parent tips

Pick the three foods your child actually eats and trace each to its farm — relevance beats completeness. Keep the watering job real: a plant that depends on them is responsibility with leaves.

Staying safe

Farms are workplaces: tractors, tools and animals are the farmer’s, not toys. Garden berries and mushrooms are never eaten without a grown-up’s yes.

This lesson pairs with the Farmer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Chef — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the restaurant kitchen door: what chefs do, how an order becomes a meal, and which kitchen jobs belong to little hands.

What is this?

A chef is a food helper who cooks meals in a restaurant kitchen for many people at once.

What does it mean?

Restaurant kitchens are busy teams: orders come in, chefs chop, cook, taste and plate, and servers carry plates out. Chefs wear aprons; many wear tall hats.

What does the child need to know?

Kitchen know-how for fours: meals are built in steps (choose → cook → plate → serve), tasting and adjusting is part of cooking, and hot things and knives are grown-up tools.

Why this matters

A restaurant visit becomes a discovery tour when your child knows the machinery behind the menu. Sous-chef jobs at home also grow brave, curious eaters.

What it teaches

Sequencing (order→cook→plate→serve), measurement and counting in real cooking, sensory vocabulary (sizzle, tangy, fresh), team-role thinking, and brave-tasting pride.

Words to learn

chefkitchenmenuorderingredientplate

Say this to your child

“"In a restaurant you choose your food from the menu, and the chef cooks it for you. Chefs taste as they cook — that is how they know it is just right."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a chef. Chefs cook food for many people in a big kitchen."
  2. Find the hat, the pans, the stove. "Everything in a kitchen has a job — just like the chef."
  3. Tell the order’s journey: you choose from the menu → the waiter tells the chef → the chef cooks and plates it → the waiter brings it out. Four beats, hand to hand.
  4. Name the smells and sounds: onions sizzle, garlic smells strong, pans clatter. Kitchens talk to your nose and ears.
  5. Assign a real sous-chef job tonight — the lesson lands in your own kitchen.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the chef cooking? What can you smell on this card (imagine!)? How many pans or bowls can you count? Is the kitchen calm or busy?

Ask your child

"Who cooks the food in a restaurant? What does the chef do first — chop, cook or plate? Which kitchen jobs are for grown-ups? What would YOU put on a menu?"

What your child can say or do

The sous-chef call-out: "Yes, chef!" And the tasting words: "Mmm, needs more…?" — trying a taste and describing it out loud.

Out in the real world

At a restaurant, watch the kitchen window: orders go in, plates come out. At home, name the chef moments: "this whisking is chef work!"

Try it together

Home restaurant: paper menus with three dishes (drawn or glued pictures), your child takes the order, "cooks" with play food or helps with the real easy dish, plates it with a leaf garnish, and announces: "Table two, ready!" Swap chef and waiter roles.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who cooks in a restaurant? What comes first — order or cooking? Which jobs are yours in our kitchen?" Chef + order-first + safe-jobs = pass.

Parent tips

Give the tasting job before the eating job — chefs taste, and tasting without pressure grows food bravery. One real task (tearing lettuce, stirring) beats an hour of toy cooking.

Staying safe

Stoves, ovens and knives are grown-up tools — a child’s kitchen jobs are washing, tearing, stirring and sprinkling. A grown-up stays in the kitchen the whole time.

This lesson pairs with the Chef flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Baker — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson follows flour to warm bread — measure, knead, wait, bake — and ends with rolls your child shaped themselves.

What is this?

A baker is a bread helper who makes bread, buns and cakes fresh every day, starting long before we wake.

What does it mean?

Bakeries have big ovens, floury tables and shelves that fill up by morning. Bakers measure, mix, knead, shape and bake — and yeast makes dough rise like a pillow.

What does the child need to know?

Bread know-how: dough needs kneading, resting (yeast works while we wait!) and a hot oven; ovens and hot trays are grown-up territory.

Why this matters

Baking is a science experiment you can eat: measuring is maths, rising is biology, kneading is muscle work. And the smell of your own bread is a memory glued for life.

What it teaches

Measurement and counting with purpose, patience in two acts (kneading and rising), sensory language (soft, springy, warm), sequencing, and fine-motor strength.

Words to learn

bakerdoughkneadyeastriseoven

Say this to your child

“"The baker mixes flour and water and kneads the dough — push, push, fold, fold. Then we wait while the yeast makes it fluffy. Then it bakes, and the whole house smells like morning."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a baker. Bakers make our bread while the whole street is still asleep."
  2. Find the bread, the oven, the flour. "Flour, water and a little yeast — that is the whole secret."
  3. Tell the dough story: mix → knead (push, fold, push, fold) → wait (the yeast puffs it up!) → shape → bake → smell → eat.
  4. Explain the mystery simply: yeast is a tiny helper that makes bubbles in the dough — that is how soft bread happens.
  5. Bake rolls together this week: your child measures, kneads and shapes; you handle the oven.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what has the baker made so far? Can you find the oven? What shape are the loaves? What time of day do you think it is — and why?

Ask your child

"What does the baker make? What does kneading feel like? Why do we wait before baking? Which part is for grown-ups?"

What your child can say or do

The knead chant: "Push, push, fold, fold!" And the waiting line: "The yeast is working — the dough is sleeping and growing."

Out in the real world

Walk past a bakery before breakfast and just breathe. At the shop, find breads by shape: long, round, braided. Every loaf was shaped by hands.

Try it together

Bake bread rolls: your child measures cups, kneads half the dough, shapes snakes, snails and knots on the tray. Watch the rise through the oven door together, then eat warm with butter. Repeat monthly — the ritual is the curriculum.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the baker make? What makes dough rise? Whose hands shape the rolls?" Bread + yeast-bubbles + your child’s = pass.

Parent tips

The waiting is the hardest and best part — set a timer and check the dough’s growth together at each beep. Flour mess is the tax on wonder; a damp cloth closes the lesson.

Staying safe

Ovens and hot trays are grown-up only. Wash hands before baking; let bread cool before small fingers tear it. No nibbling raw dough with yeast.

This lesson pairs with the Baker flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Gardener — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson walks the gardener’s round — planting, weeding, watering, trimming — and ends with a plant your child adopts and owns.

What is this?

A gardener is a plant helper who takes care of gardens and parks so flowers bloom and trees stay healthy.

What does it mean?

Gardeners plant seeds and seedlings, pull weeds (plant robbers!), water, trim hedges, feed the soil with compost and sweep the paths.

What does the child need to know?

Plant needs in child-size: water, sunshine, soil and time. And the gardener’s secret: weeds steal the water, so out they come.

Why this matters

Gardens run on patience — nothing rushes a seed. A child who waters a plant daily learns responsibility the honest way: something alive depends on them.

What it teaches

Daily-care responsibility, plant-need reasoning, patience across weeks, fine motor (pinching weeds, gentle watering), and nature observation habits.

Words to learn

gardenerseedweedcompostbloomroots

Say this to your child

“"The gardener waters the plants and pulls the weeds. Water, sunshine, soil and time — then one day: a flower! Growing things cannot be rushed, and that is the fun."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a gardener. Gardeners help plants grow big and strong."
  2. Find the plants, the watering can, the tools. "Every tool has a job — watering, digging, trimming."
  3. Name the plant’s needs with your fingers: water (rain fingers), sun (arms up), soil (wiggle toes), time (tap wrist).
  4. Introduce the villain kindly: "Weeds are plant robbers — they drink the water. The gardener pulls them out so flowers can eat."
  5. Adopt a plant today: one pot, one name, one job — your child’s.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the gardener doing first? Can you find a flower and a leaf? What does the soil look like — wet or dry? What tool would you pick up first?

Ask your child

"What do plants need to grow? Why does the gardener pull weeds? What is your plant’s name? How will you know it is thirsty?"

What your child can say or do

The needs list, counted on fingers: "Water, sun, soil, time." And the care report each morning: "My plant is… (dry/droopy/happy)."

Out in the real world

Walk the park as gardener-detective: fresh mulch here, trimmed hedge there, new tulips — someone did all of it. Community gardens love little visitors.

Try it together

Adopt-a-plant: one sturdy pot plant (herbs are forgiving), named by your child. Their job: check leaves, test soil with one finger, water gently with a small can. A ribbon measures growth; a calendar tick marks the care.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do plants need? Why do we pull weeds? Whose job is our plant?" Needs + weeds + theirs = pass.

Parent tips

Choose forgiving plants — mint, geraniums, spider plants. A wilted plant is not a failure, it is a clue: droopy = thirsty, yellow = too much love (water). Gardeners solve problems; so can fours.

Staying safe

Wash hands after soil play and wear gloves for digging. Some plants — berries, mushrooms, sap — are not for touching or tasting: ask a grown-up first, always.

This lesson pairs with the Gardener flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Veterinarian — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the animal clinic: how vets examine patients who cannot talk, what animals’ bodies tell us, and how to be gentle with real creatures.

What is this?

A veterinarian is an animal doctor who helps pets and farm animals stay healthy and heal when they are hurt.

What does it mean?

Vets work in animal clinics. They examine, vaccinate, treat wounds and teach owners how to care for their animals — from kittens to cows.

What does the child need to know?

Animal-care basics for fours: animals cannot say where it hurts, so we watch them carefully; we ask the owner before touching any animal; pets need quiet, food, water and gentle hands.

Why this matters

Fours run on animal love. Channelling it through the vet’s watching skills builds real empathy — and the ask-before-petting rule prevents the bites that end friendships with dogs.

What it teaches

Observation skills (body-language reading), gentleness control, asking permission, care routines for living things, and job-vocabulary (clinic, patient, check-up).

Words to learn

veterinarianvetpatientgentlecheck-uppaws

Say this to your child

“"The veterinarian is an animal doctor. Animals cannot tell us where it hurts, so the vet watches carefully and checks gently. And we always ask before we pet any animal."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a veterinarian — an animal doctor. When a pet is sick, the vet helps."
  2. Find the animals, the tools, the clinic. "The vet listens to hearts, looks in ears and checks paws — just like your doctor."
  3. Explain the vet’s superpower: "Animals cannot say ‘my tummy hurts’. So vets watch very carefully: how does the animal move? Eat? Sleep?"
  4. Teach the two animal rules: always ask the owner before touching, and be gentle — soft voice, soft hands.
  5. Open the teddy clinic and practise the whole visit.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: which animals can you find? What is the vet doing — listening, looking, wrapping? What is on the table? Can you find an animal that looks calm?

Ask your child

"Who is an animal doctor? Why do vets watch instead of ask? What do we say before touching a dog? What does a pet need every day?"

What your child can say or do

The permission line: "May I pet your dog, please?" And the clinic line: "Let me check you gently — tell me if it hurts."

Out in the real world

Vet-visit stories from your own pets or friends’ pets. On walks, watch dogs from afar and read tails: wagging loose = happy, stiff and tucked = give space.

Try it together

Teddy pet clinic: booking desk (paper appointments), waiting room (cushions), exam table (couch arm). Your child the vet checks ears, paws and heart (gentle tummy taps), wraps a tissue bandage and gives a "kind words" prescription. You bring in the "worried owner" voice.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who is an animal doctor? What do we ask before petting? How do gentle vet hands touch?" Vet + ask-first + soft hands = pass.

Parent tips

Read animal body language together at the park: stiff body, tucked tail, whale-eye — all "space please" signs. Praise asking behaviour more than petting itself.

Staying safe

Always ask the owner before touching any animal, even friendly-looking ones. Never disturb animals while they eat or sleep, and never touch strange cats, dogs or wildlife.

This lesson pairs with the Veterinarian flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Scientist — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the scientist’s loop — observe, guess, test, look again — and runs a first experiment with jars and a spoon.

What is this?

A scientist is a discovery helper who asks "why?" and finds answers by testing carefully.

What does it mean?

Scientists work in labs, outdoors and in space. They watch closely, make a guess (a hypothesis), run experiments, measure what happens and share results with other scientists.

What does the child need to know?

The scientific loop in child words: LOOK, GUESS, TRY, LOOK AGAIN. Guessing is not cheating — it is the first step of every real discovery.

Why this matters

The scientist mindset is the gift that keeps giving: "let’s find out" beats "because I said so", and a flopped experiment becomes "interesting!" instead of failure.

What it teaches

Curiosity routines, guess-before-test inhibition (thinking before doing), observation vocabulary, outcome reasoning, and flop-resilience.

Words to learn

scientistexperimentguessobservediscoverresult

Say this to your child

“"A scientist looks, guesses, tries and looks again. If we wonder about something, we can be scientists too: we guess first, then we find out!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a scientist. Scientists find out why things happen by testing them."
  2. Find the tools: what might be in those flasks and papers? "Scientists write everything down."
  3. Teach the loop with your hands: eyes (look), finger to chin (guess), hands (try), eyes again (look again!).
  4. Explain the golden rule: "A guess is a good beginning. Scientists guess FIRST, then test — the test tells the truth."
  5. Run the three-jar experiment now: guess, tap, listen, compare.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the scientist holding or mixing? What might be inside the jars? Is the scientist writing something down? What colour is the "science" on this card?

Ask your child

"What does a scientist do first — guess or test?" "What are YOU wondering about this week?" "What happened in our jar experiment? What would you try next?"

What your child can say or do

The loop chant: "Look, guess, try, look again!" And the flop line, borrowed from every lab: "Interesting! Let’s try it another way."

Out in the real world

Scientists are everywhere: weather presenters, bakers testing recipes, gardeners testing soil. When anyone says "let’s test it", name it: "that is science!"

Try it together

Three-jar sound test: jars filled full, half and empty of water. Before tapping: everyone guesses which sounds highest. Tap with a spoon, listen, line them up low-to-high. Then the real experiment: can you play a tune?

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a scientist do first? What comes after the guess? What did our jars show us?" Look-guess-try + a remembered result = pass.

Parent tips

Write down your child’s guesses like a real lab book — being taken seriously fuels scientists. Say "interesting!" to surprises, including messy ones: data is data.

Staying safe

Kitchen-lab rules: nothing gets tasted, goggles (or swimming glasses) for anything splashy, and a grown-up runs any experiment with heat or liquids.

This lesson pairs with the Scientist flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Dentist — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the dental chair familiar before your child sits in it — what the dentist does, what the tools do, and the brushing routine that keeps visits easy.

What is this?

A dentist is a tooth helper who checks teeth, cleans them, fixes small holes and teaches everyone the best brushing moves.

What does it mean?

Dental clinics have a big reclining chair, a bright lamp, a mirror on a stick and tiny scrapers. A dental nurse helps beside the dentist.

What does the child need to know?

Tooth know-how: dentists count and clean teeth; check-ups are mostly looking; brushing happens morning and night with a pea-sized dab of paste.

Why this matters

Dental fear is learned from adults. An honest, specific story — chair, lamp, mirror, count — plus a solid brushing habit keeps first visits boring, which is exactly right.

What it teaches

Health-routine ownership (the brushing habit), counting practice on a real mouthful, honest-body-talk vocabulary, and calm waiting skills.

Words to learn

dentistcheck-upcleanbrushtoothpastecavity

Say this to your child

“"The dentist counts your teeth and keeps them strong. We brush morning and night so the dentist finds happy, clean teeth. If anything feels strange in the chair, you tell the dentist — they will stop and explain."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a dentist. Dentists keep our teeth healthy and strong."
  2. Find the chair, the lamp, the tools. "The chair lies down like a rocket seat, and the lamp is a little sun."
  3. Tell the check-up in order, honestly: lie back → open wide → the dentist counts and looks with a tiny mirror → maybe a clean and polish → done, with a sticker.
  4. Be honest about the odd bits: the mirror is cold, the polish buzzes, holding your mouth open is strange work — and you can always raise a hand to say so.
  5. Brush twice a day together: outside circles, inside, chewing tops — two minutes, song optional but recommended.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the dentist looking at? Can you find the little mirror? What is the lamp for? Does the patient look calm or worried?

Ask your child

"Who keeps our teeth strong? What does the dentist do first at a check-up? How many teeth can you count in the mirror? When do we brush?"

What your child can say or do

The open-wide line: "Ahh!" with five seconds of stillness. And the honest line: "That feels cold/funny" — practised on a teddy first.

Out in the real world

Count teeth in the mirror after brushing — most fours have twenty. Spot other people brushing in books and films; dentist talk stays light and daily, not pre-visit only.

Try it together

Teddy dental clinic: your child the dentist, toothbrush for a teddy with big paper teeth. Count aloud ("one, two… twenty!"), brush the sugar bugs away, then swap — you brush your child’s real teeth while they do the dentist-voice. Two minutes, twice a day.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the dentist do at a check-up? When do we brush? What do we say if something feels strange in the chair?" Count + twice-a-day + tell-the-dentist = pass.

Parent tips

Brush FOR them until about six — their technique cannot yet do the job alone; let them "finish" for pride. Book check-ups for mornings when possible; tired teeth-jaws clamp.

Staying safe

Pea-sized toothpaste only, and teach spitting — toothpaste is for brushing, not swallowing. Only grown-ups floss little teeth.

This lesson pairs with the Dentist flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Optometrist — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson normalises eye tests before the first one: what the optometrist does, why some eyes wear glasses, and how the test works as a game.

What is this?

An optometrist is an eye helper who checks how well eyes see and finds glasses when eyes need extra help.

What does it mean?

Eye clinics have a big chair, a chart of letters and pictures far away, a little light to look into eyes, and drawers of trial glasses to try.

What does the child need to know?

Eye know-how: eye tests are games of naming what you see; some eyes need glasses to see clearly; glasses are helpers, like helmets for vision.

Why this matters

Children with blurry vision often do not know — blur is their normal. Making eye tests ordinary and game-shaped means early help instead of years of squinting.

What it teaches

Self-report skills ("it is clearer now!"), one-eye-at-a-time control, naming-and-matching practice, and the normalisation reflex: glasses = ordinary as socks.

Words to learn

optometristeyesglassesblurrycleareye chart

Say this to your child

“"The optometrist checks how your eyes see. You look at pictures far away and say what they are. If your eyes want extra help, you get glasses — and then the world looks sharp."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an optometrist. They check eyes so everything looks clear and easy to see."
  2. Find the chart, the glasses, the chair. "Some pictures on the chart are big and some are tiny — the optometrist asks what you can see."
  3. Explain glasses kindly: "Sometimes the eye’s window needs a little help. Glasses are that help — like goggles for seeing."
  4. Play the eye-test game: cover one eye, name shapes far away, swap eyes. Both eyes get a turn.
  5. If a real test is booked, tell the story in advance: chair, chart, "which one is clearer, one or two?"

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is on the eye chart? What is the optometrist holding near the eyes? Can you find glasses on this card? Who is wearing them?

Ask your child

"Who checks our eyes? What do we do at an eye test? What do glasses do? Who do you know who wears glasses?"

What your child can say or do

The test lines: "I can see a boat/star/apple!" And the honesty line that matters most: "This one is clearer!" — eyes get a vote.

Out in the real world

Glasses-spotting on every outing: the baker, the storybook bear, Grandpa. The more ordinary glasses look, the happier any future glasses day will be.

Try it together

Wall chart game: stick shapes and letters at kid height, step back three steps, name them — one eye, then the other, then both. Your child "tests" you next. (Play, not diagnosis — real checks belong to the optometrist.)

Understanding check

Ask: "Who checks our eyes? What do we say during the test? What do glasses do?" Optometrist + say-what-you-see + helpers = pass.

Parent tips

Watch for squinting, head-tilting, sitting very close to screens or books, and "my eyes are tired" — all gentle reasons to book a real check. Frame any first visit as a game day.

This lesson pairs with the Optometrist flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sanitation Worker — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson follows the bin truck’s route: who empties our bins, where "away" actually is, and how sorting recyclables becomes a daily family game.

What is this?

A sanitation worker is a cleaning helper who collects our bins and waste so the neighborhood stays clean and healthy.

What does it mean?

Sanitation workers drive big collection trucks along a route, lifting and emptying bins — some trucks have robot arms! They collect recycling separately so it can be made into new things.

What does the child need to know?

Waste know-how for fours: rubbish does not vanish — helpers carry it away; recycling goes in its own bin; trucks are big, loud and cannot see small people.

Why this matters

Every child adores bin day. Naming the workers and the route turns adoration into gratitude and habits — and 'throw it away' becomes 'put it in the bin for the helpers'.

What it teaches

Sorting and classifying (the recycling game is real cognitive work), calendar sense (which day is bin day?), gratitude for invisible work, and truck-safety habits.

Words to learn

sanitation workerrubbishrecyclingbinroutecollect

Say this to your child

“"The sanitation worker keeps our street clean by taking the rubbish away. Recycling goes in its own bin so it can become something new — and on bin day we watch from far back and wave."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a sanitation worker. They take our rubbish away and keep our street clean."
  2. Find the truck, the bins, the lifting arms. "The truck is strong enough to lift our whole bin — look!"
  3. Follow the journey: bin by our gate → truck lifts and tips → the rubbish rides away → recycling gets sorted and made NEW.
  4. Introduce the sorting idea: paper, plastic, everything else — three bins, three teams.
  5. Learn bin day: mark it on the calendar, put the bin out together the night before.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the truck lifting? Can you find the driver and the helper? Which bin is for recycling? What colours do you see on the truck?

Ask your child

"Who empties our bins? Where does rubbish go after the truck? What goes in the recycling bin? What day is bin day?"

What your child can say or do

The sort call-out while playing: "Paper team! Plastic team!" And the bin-day line: "The truck is coming — let’s watch from the window."

Out in the real world

Bin day from the window (safely far back): lifting, tipping, crushing — theatre! Visit a recycling point and let your child post bottles into the bank; the clunk is deeply satisfying.

Try it together

Three-bin sorting game: clean "waste" from the recycling drawer (paper, card, plastic bottles). Three boxes, relay race, count each team’s score. Wrong bin? No scolding — "rescue it!" is part of the game.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who takes our rubbish away? Where does recycling go? What do we do when the truck comes — run to it or watch from far back?" Workers + recycling + far-back = pass.

Parent tips

Praise the invisible: "someone emptied six streets before breakfast — that is strong, kind work". Recycling confusion is normal; keep the rule simple and let your council’s guide settle the details.

Staying safe

Collection trucks are huge with blind spots — watch from the window or far back on the kerb, never near or behind the truck. Wash hands after touching bins.

This lesson pairs with the Sanitation Worker flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Hairdresser — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson narrates the whole haircut — cape, mist, snip, buzz, mirror spin — so the real salon chair feels like a story your child already knows.

What is this?

A hairdresser is a grooming helper who washes, cuts and styles hair so people leave the salon feeling great.

What does it mean?

Salons have special up-down chairs, big mirrors, spray bottles, combs, scissors and clippers. Hairdressers listen first, then cut carefully and sweep up after.

What does the child need to know?

Salon know-how: we sit very still while the hairdresser works; tools are sharp or hot and belong to the hairdresser; telling the hairdresser what we want is part of the job.

Why this matters

For children who flinch at haircuts, the fear is the unknown: sounds, capes, stillness. Narrating the process turns each strange element into a chapter they can predict.

What it teaches

Sitting-still stamina (a real self-regulation win), process vocabulary, asking-for-what-you-want, sensory prediction (buzz, mist, snip), and body-care identity.

Words to learn

hairdressersaloncapescissorsstyleclippers

Say this to your child

“"The hairdresser asks what we want, puts the cape on, and cuts slowly and carefully. We sit still like statues, watch in the mirror — and then the big spin to see the new hairdo!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a hairdresser. They cut and style hair so we look and feel great."
  2. Find the scissors, the mirror, the chair. "The chair goes up and down — that is the fun part."
  3. Tell the haircut story in order: choose the style → cape on → mist of water → snip with scissors or buzz with clippers → dry → mirror spin → "all done!"
  4. Be honest about sensations: the cape feels tickly, the spray is cold, the clippers buzz your hand’s favourite song. Naming makes them friendly.
  5. Rehearse with the teddy salon before any real appointment.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the hairdresser doing? Can you find the mirror and the cape? Is the customer sitting still? What would YOU ask the hairdresser for?

Ask your child

"Who cuts hair? What does the cape do? Why do we sit very still? What would you tell the hairdresser about your haircut?"

What your child can say or do

The order line: "A short cut please, with a spiky top!" And the stillness challenge: "Statue sit!" — five seconds, building up.

Out in the real world

Narrate your own salon visits; point out salons on walks. Home haircuts: name the sound of the scissors and the mist of the bottle as "salon sounds".

Try it together

Teddy salon: doll in the "chair", paper cape with a towel collar, yarn or paper-strip hair to "cut" with play scissors, a comb, the big finish — mirror spin and "ooh la la!" Swap roles; the barber gets a turn in the chair too.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who cuts hair? What do we do in the chair? Whose hands use the scissors?" Hairdresser + statue-still + theirs = pass.

Parent tips

Book morning appointments and say what will happen in order beforehand. For clipper-fear, let them feel the buzz on their own arm first — vibration is friendlier than surprise. Bring the teddy; even superheroes need haircuts.

Staying safe

Real scissors, clippers and hot dryers are hairdresser tools only. In the salon, hands stay in laps — no reaching for tools, no grabbing the cape.

This lesson pairs with the Hairdresser flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).
