LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Carpenter — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson follows one plank’s journey into furniture — measure, cut, sand, join — and hands your child the carpenter’s golden rule.

What is this?

A carpenter is a building helper who makes things from wood: furniture, doors, shelves and frames.

What does it mean?

Carpenters work in workshops and on sites with planks, saws, hammers, screwdrivers, sandpaper and a tape measure. Their rule: measure twice, cut once.

What does the child need to know?

Woodworking basics for fours: measure first, cut second; wood can be sanded smooth; real cutting tools are grown-up tools — children measure, hold and sand.

Why this matters

Carpentry turns numbers into objects: a length, a half, a corner. Few lessons make maths as holdable as building something that actually stands.

What it teaches

Measurement sense, sequencing (plan→measure→cut→join→sand), precision pride, hand strength and control, plus tool respect that transfers to every workshop.

Words to learn

carpenterplankmeasuresawsandjoin

Say this to your child

“"A carpenter builds with wood. We measure first — twice! — then cut, then sand until it is smooth as a spoon. Real saws are for grown-ups; measuring and sanding are for us."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a carpenter. Carpenters build with wood — chairs, shelves, birdhouses!"
  2. Find the tools and the wood. "That measuring tape tells the carpenter exactly where to cut."
  3. Tell the build story: choose what to make → measure the wood → cut (grown-up) → sand it smooth → join the pieces → stand back and admire.
  4. Teach the golden rule out loud: "Measure twice, cut once — because you cannot un-cut wood!"
  5. Give your child the child-safe jobs on a real build: measuring, holding, sanding.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the carpenter making? Which tools can you name? What does the measuring tape say? What has already been built on this card?

Ask your child

"What does a carpenter build with? Why measure twice? Which tools are for grown-ups only? What could we build together?"

What your child can say or do

The rule, chanted: "Measure twice, cut once!" And the builder’s report: "I measured it and held it and sanded it smooth."

Out in the real world

Furniture safari at home: find three wooden things and guess how they were joined — nails, screws, clever shapes. Woodworking shows and makers’ fairs are field trips.

Try it together

Offcut workshop: a box of smooth wood offcuts, string, and child-safe sandpaper. Your child sands, sorts by size and builds — a boat, a robot, a doll bed — joined with string and big blocks. Real tools appear only with a grown-up: one nail, one hammer, one board, four hands.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a carpenter build with? What is the golden rule? Which jobs are yours on a real build?" Wood + measure-twice + sanding = pass.

Parent tips

The sanding station is the magic — repetitive, sensory, genuinely useful. Keep offcuts in a dedicated box; loose wood is the best open-ended toy in the house.

Staying safe

Saws, drills and nails are grown-up tools. Around any workbench: safety glasses on, hands clear, and a grown-up runs every cut and hammer strike.

This lesson pairs with the Carpenter flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Construction Worker — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the biggest sequencing story in town — how a hole in the ground becomes a house — and puts your child in the hard hat.

What is this?

A construction worker is a building helper who builds houses, roads, bridges and schools.

What does it mean?

Construction sites have cranes, diggers, cement mixers and brick stacks. Workers dig foundations, pour concrete, lay bricks, fit beams and check walls — each trade builds one part.

What does the child need to know?

Building know-how: big things are built in ORDER — foundations, walls, roof, inside; every worker wears a hard hat and hi-vis because sites are real workplaces; sites are never playgrounds.

Why this matters

Watching a site change week by week is a living sequencing puzzle. Naming the order and the machines feeds the digger-madness phase with real words.

What it teaches

Sequencing (the foundation of maths!), machine vocabulary, cause-effect (cranes lift because…) patience across long builds, and rule-respect for real workplaces.

Words to learn

construction workersitefoundationcranebrickshard hat

Say this to your child

“"Construction workers build big things step by step: first the foundations, then the walls, then the roof. The hard hat keeps every builder safe — and building sites are for builders only."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a construction worker. They build the houses, roads and bridges we all use."
  2. Find the hard hat and hi-vis vest. "The hat protects the head; the bright vest says HERE I AM to the machines."
  3. Tell the build order with stacked hands: foundations (the hidden feet) → walls (brick by brick) → roof (the umbrella) → inside (doors, paints, floors).
  4. Name two machines and their jobs: the crane lifts, the digger scoops, the mixer spins.
  5. Find a real site on your walk (from the safe side!) and guess today’s chapter: digging? walls? roof?

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is being built on this card? Can you find the crane or the bricks? What is the worker wearing? What do you think gets built first?

Ask your child

"What gets built first — walls or foundations? What does the crane do? Why do builders wear hard hats? What is being built near our house?"

What your child can say or do

The build chant: "Foundations, walls, roof!" And the site rule: "Building sites are for builders — we watch from the fence."

Out in the real world

Walk past sites (safely) weekly and name today’s chapter. Books with cut-away houses show the hidden order — foundations are always the surprise.

Try it together

Build-a-house game: foundations (blocks flat on the rug) → walls (bricks up) → roof (cardboard) → furniture (dolls move in). Do it wrong on purpose — roof first! — and let your child the foreman correct you.

Understanding check

Ask: "What gets built first? Why do builders wear hats? Can we play on a building site?" Foundations + hard hat + no = pass.

Parent tips

Learn the machines your child loves by their real names — excavator, not "digger-digger". Sequence talk ("what came first?") is quietly training maths-story brains.

Staying safe

Building sites are never playgrounds — keep out, even when they look empty or quiet. Machines and materials are workers’ only. Hard hats and hi-vis are real safety gear.

This lesson pairs with the Construction Worker flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Architect — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the architect’s superpower — imagining first, drawing second, building last — and ends with a floor plan of your own home.

What is this?

An architect is a design helper who draws the plans for buildings before the builders build them.

What does it mean?

Architects work in studios with rulers, pencils and computers. They talk to the people who will use the building, draw every room, door and window, and make models to test ideas.

What does the child need to know?

Design know-how for fours: we THINK, then DRAW, then BUILD; plans show where things go; changing the drawing is easier than changing the building.

Why this matters

Architecture links empathy to maths: who lives here? where does the light come from? Draw-first-build-second is also the peaceful sibling of "measure twice, cut once".

What it teaches

Plan-before-do thinking, spatial reasoning (rooms, doors, paths), drawing-to-communicate ideas, perspective-taking (who will use this room?), and revision pride.

Words to learn

architectplandesignfloor planmodeldraw

Say this to your child

“"The architect draws the house before anyone builds it. Draw first, build second! Where will your room go? Where does the sun come in?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an architect. They draw the house first — then the builders build it."
  2. Find the paper, the ruler, the drawings. "Every line on the plan is a wall, a door or a window."
  3. Tell the architect’s loop: listen to what people need → draw the plan → change it and change it → hand it to the builders.
  4. Compare sizes: "On the plan, your bedroom is this big rectangle. A plan is a house map!"
  5. Draw your home’s floor plan together — then build it in blocks.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the architect drawing? Can you find a ruler or a plan? What rooms might be in this building? What would YOUR dream house need?

Ask your child

"Who draws houses before they are built? What does a plan show us? What comes first — drawing or building? Where would you put the garden?"

What your child can say or do

The loop chant: "Think, draw, build!" And the designer line: "On my plan, this room is the…" — narrating their own drawing.

Out in the real world

Spot architect work everywhere: your street’s different roofs, the library’s big windows, the park’s curvy paths — every one was drawn first.

Try it together

Floor-plan studio: draw your home as big rectangles (rooms), lines (doors), squares (windows) — no art quality required, ideas only. Then build it in blocks, matching the plan. Add one dream room: a cake room is a valid architectural choice.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who draws buildings first? What does a plan show? What comes first — think, draw or build?" Architect + house-map + think-draw-build = pass.

Parent tips

Value the drawing over the beauty — architects communicate, they do not decorate. When a block tower falls, ask "what would you change on the plan?" — revision is the real skill.

This lesson pairs with the Architect flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Electrician — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson names the person who tames electricity and installs the one rule that matters: children never touch plugs, wires or sockets.

What is this?

An electrician is a power helper who works with wires and electricity — installing and fixing the power that lights our homes.

What does it mean?

Electricians run wires through walls, fit plugs, switches and lights, and test circuits with meters. They wear special gloves and follow strict safety rules, because electricity is powerful.

What does the child need to know?

Electricity rules for fours: sockets, wires and plugs are never touched or poked; water and electricity never mix; every spark, tingle or funny smell gets reported to a grown-up immediately.

Why this matters

"But WHY not?" deserves a real answer: electricity travels in wires like water in pipes, it is invisible, and it can hurt — so the electrician is the only one who opens those pipes.

What it teaches

Hazard recognition, rule-with-reasoning (which sticks!), report-reflex training, sorting skills (battery vs plug power), and respect for invisible forces.

Words to learn

electricianelectricitywireplugsocketsafety

Say this to your child

“"Electricians are the only ones who work with wires and plugs. We never touch sockets or cables — electricity is strong and invisible. If anything sparks or smells funny, we tell a grown-up straight away."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an electrician. They work with electricity — the power that lights our lamps."
  2. Find the wires and tools. "Electricians wear special gloves and use testers — electricity is powerful, so they are careful."
  3. Explain it simply: electricity flows in wires like water in pipes. The electrician is the only person who may open those pipes.
  4. Install the rule with its reason: we never poke sockets or chew cables — not because we are in trouble, but because electricity BITES.
  5. Do the power hunt: what in this room runs on batteries, and what runs on plugs?

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the electrician holding? Can you find wires or a tester? What safety things is the electrician wearing? What might the electrician be fixing?

Ask your child

"Who may fix plugs and wires? Why do we never poke sockets? What runs on batteries in our home? What do we do if a cable looks broken?"

What your child can say or do

The rule, in full: "Sockets and wires are never for touching — I tell a grown-up instead." And the report line: "Come look — something is sparking/broken!"

Out in the real world

When an electrician visits, let your child watch the testing meter from a safe spot. Battery toys vs plug toys sorting happens naturally every playday.

Try it together

Power detective: tour one room and sort everything into "battery team" (torch, remote, toy) and "plug team" (lamp, TV, kettle). Draw both teams. The plug team gets a red paper "grown-ups only" sticker — drawn by your child.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who may touch wires and plugs? What do we do if a cable is broken? Can electricity and water play together?" Electrician-only + tell-a-grown-up + never = pass.

Parent tips

Answer "why?" with the water-in-pipes picture every time — reasoning survives better than prohibition. Never scare with horror stories; a calm, factual "electricity can hurt, so we have rules" is stronger.

Staying safe

Never poke sockets, chew cables or put anything into plugs. Water and electricity never mix — no bath toys near plugs. Report every spark, tingle or burnt smell immediately.

This lesson pairs with the Electrician flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Plumber — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson uncovers the hidden water roads under your home: who installs them, who fixes them, and why even a tiny drip gets reported.

What is this?

A plumber is a water helper who works with pipes — installing sinks and taps, fixing leaks and keeping water flowing where it should.

What does it mean?

Plumbers crawl under sinks and along pipes with wrenches, tape, seals and a plunger. They fit pipes, fix blockages and test that water goes the right way — and only there.

What does the child need to know?

Water-system basics: clean water arrives through pipes, used water leaves through other pipes; drips and puddles get reported early; drains are not for poking things into.

Why this matters

Plumbing is invisible infrastructure your child uses ten times a day. Naming the system — and the person who fixes it — turns "where does the water GO?" into a story.

What it teaches

Systems thinking (in-pipes, out-pipes), cause-effect reasoning (drip today, puddle tomorrow), reporting responsibility, bath-time engineering play, and home-mapping.

Words to learn

plumberpipetapleakdrainwrench

Say this to your child

“"The plumber takes care of our water. Clean water arrives in pipes, used water leaves in pipes. If a tap drips or the floor is wet, we tell a grown-up so the plumber can fix it soon."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a plumber. Plumbers take care of our water pipes."
  2. Find the pipes, the wrench, the tap. "The wrench turns big nuts that hold pipes together."
  3. Follow the water’s journey: pipe brings clean water to the tap → we use it → used water leaves through the drain → more pipes carry it away. Two directions, one system!
  4. Teach the drip rule: "A tiny drip is the pipe saying ‘fix me soon’ — we always tell a grown-up."
  5. Count the taps and pipes in your home; find the stop tap with a grown-up.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the plumber fixing? Can you find a wrench or a pipe? Is the water running or dripping? What tools would a plumber carry?

Ask your child

"Who fixes our pipes? Where does water come from — and where does it go? What do we do about a drip? What should never go into a drain?"

What your child can say or do

The report line: "Drip drip — come look, the tap needs the plumber!" And the drain rule: "Only water goes down the drain."

Out in the real world

Under-sink safari (cabinet open, together): find the U-bend and the pipes. Every tap and toilet is plumbing your child already uses — name the system each time.

Try it together

Bath pipe-works: pool-noodle pipes cut in half, funnels, cups and jugs. Build routes from the tap-end to the bucket-end: which path carries the most water? Where does it leak? You are doing real plumbing.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who fixes pipes and leaks? What do we do when we see a drip? Do toys go down the drain?" Plumber + report + never = pass.

Parent tips

Report drips the same day and let your child hear you phone the plumber — early reporting is the actual lesson. Keep a small "fix-it list" on the fridge; your child can draw the dripping tap as item one.

Staying safe

Wet floors are slippery — report every puddle, do not splash-test it. Nothing poked into drains or taps, ever; that is the plumber’s job with real tools.

This lesson pairs with the Plumber flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Mechanic — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson demystifies the garage: what mechanics do, how they find what is wrong, and which parts of the car your child can safely inspect.

What is this?

A mechanic is a machine helper who fixes cars — finding what is wrong and making it right again.

What does it mean?

Mechanics work in garages with car lifts, ramps, spanners and computers that talk to the car. They change oil and tyres, listen for strange noises and check brakes and lights.

What does the child need to know?

Car-care basics: cars need check-ups like people; mechanics LISTEN and test before fixing; the garage is a workshop — waiting area only for children.

Why this matters

Cars are mysterious but learnable: noises have meanings, parts have names. A child who has inspected a tyre meets the mechanic as a colleague, not a stranger.

What it teaches

Diagnosis thinking (symptom → cause), part vocabulary, machine empathy ("the car is telling us something"), observation skills, and workshop-safety respect.

Words to learn

mechanicgarageenginetyrebrakeslift

Say this to your child

“"The mechanic listens to the car and finds what is wrong. Cars need check-ups too — oil, tyres and brakes. Mechanics know every sound a car can make."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a mechanic. Mechanics fix cars so they run safely."
  2. Find the lift, the wheels, the tools. "The lift raises the whole car so the mechanic can see underneath!"
  3. Tell the garage story: the car makes a funny noise → the mechanic listens and tests → finds the problem → fixes it → the car drives home happy. Four beats.
  4. Name the big checks: oil (the car’s juice), tyres (the shoes), brakes (the stoppers), lights (the eyes).
  5. Inspect the family car together — parked, engine off, keys away.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the mechanic doing — lifting, listening, fixing? Which parts of the car can you see? What tools do you recognise? Is the car up in the air or on the ground?

Ask your child

"Who fixes cars? How does the mechanic find the problem? What do tyres do? Why do cars need check-ups?"

What your child can say or do

The garage line: "My car is making a funny noise — please check it!" And the inspection report: "The tyres are fat and strong. The lights work!"

Out in the real world

Park visits become inspections: fat tyres or flat? Lights on both sides? The bonnet’s warmth after a drive is engine talk waiting to happen.

Try it together

Tyre and light check (parked, engine off, handbrake on): press a tyre wall — firm! Count the lights, find the mirrors, listen to the door thunk. Your child reports like a real mechanic: "All checked, all good!"

Understanding check

Ask: "Who fixes cars? What do tyres and brakes do? Where do children wait in a garage?" Mechanic + stoppers/goes + waiting area = pass.

Parent tips

Garage visits turn real when your child names three things mechanics check — most mechanics will happily show the lift for an interested four-year-old. Toy car "garages" at home run the same story on small scale.

Staying safe

Garages are workshops: cars on lifts, tools and fluids are not toys. Children stay in the waiting area — and nobody ever crawls under a car, not even to look.

This lesson pairs with the Mechanic flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · COMMUNITY HELPERS & OUR NEIGHBORHOOD · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bus Mechanic — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson scales up from one car to a whole fleet: the depot where buses sleep, the mechanic who checks every one, and big-vehicle safety rules.

What is this?

A bus mechanic is a big-vehicle helper who keeps a whole fleet of buses safe, checked and ready each morning.

What does it mean?

The depot is a giant garage where buses park, get washed, fuelled and fixed. Bus mechanics test brakes, check doors and ramps, change huge tyres and give every bus a safety check before it carries people again.

What does the child need to know?

Depot know-how: a fleet means EVERY bus must be safe, not just one; big vehicles have big blind spots; we never climb on, under or behind parked buses.

Why this matters

The fleet idea stretches thinking: dozens of buses, every single one, every single day. It is responsibility at scale — and depot pits and lifts are unforgettable machinery.

What it teaches

Scale comparison (car vs bus parts), systematic checking (one bus, then the next), big-vehicle safety habits, fleet-and-route thinking, and inspection vocabulary.

Words to learn

bus mechanicdepotfleetsafety checkbrakesinspection

Say this to your child

“"Bus mechanics check every bus before it drives: big brakes, big tyres, big doors. If every bus passes the check, everyone rides safely. We never climb on parked buses — even sleeping ones."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a bus mechanic. They check every bus so every ride is safe."
  2. Find the big bus, the lift, the tools. "Everything on a bus is bigger — the tyres, the wrenches, the sounds!"
  3. Explain the fleet: "In the depot sleep MANY buses. The mechanic checks them one by one — brakes, doors, lights, ramps — before any bus carries people."
  4. Contrast with the car garage: one car today; a whole fleet every morning. That is a big, important job.
  5. Set the big-vehicle rule: parked buses are sleeping giants — we never climb on, under or behind them.

Look closer at the picture

Ask: what is the mechanic checking? How many buses can you find? What is bigger on a bus than on a car? Where do you think buses sleep at night?

Ask your child

"Who checks the buses? What gets checked — doors, brakes, what else? Why must EVERY bus be checked? Do we climb on parked buses?"

What your child can say or do

The depot line: "Every bus checked, every bus safe!" And the big-vehicle rule: "Parked buses are sleeping giants — we keep away."

Out in the real world

Any bus ride gains a layer: "the mechanic checked these brakes." Depot spotting from the road (far back); some depots run open days — pit views are jaw-droppers.

Try it together

Depot inspection: line up toy buses. Your child the mechanic checks each: brakes (block behind wheels), doors (open-close count), lights (draw them glowing), ramp (fold-out). Stamp a paper "PASSED" per bus — the whole fleet must pass before the route starts.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who keeps buses safe? What does the mechanic check? Do we climb on parked buses?" Bus mechanic + brakes-doors-lights + never = pass.

Parent tips

Scale talk is the gold: "the mechanic’s wrench is THIS long for bus nuts!" Compare car and bus side by side. Fleet-checking games quietly teach systematic, complete work — the scholar’s habit.

Staying safe

Depots and parked buses are real workshops with pits and heavy vehicles — never climb on, under or behind any bus. Watch big vehicles from far back: they cannot see small people.

This lesson pairs with the Bus Mechanic flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood (Class 33).

COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Doctor — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace DOCTOR, match the doctor to the stethoscope, bandage and thermometer, circle the healthy habits, count the medicine bottles and draw one way you care for your body.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a doctor’s tools are for, which everyday habits keep bodies healthy, and how to read and write the word DOCTOR.

Knowledge to have ready: Your child needs a little vocabulary first: a doctor helps sick and hurt people, a stethoscope listens to heartbeats, a bandage protects a healing cut, and a thermometer checks temperature. Say each tool’s name before the pencil starts.

Why this activity matters: Doctors become familiar instead of frightening when children meet their tools on paper first. The healthy-habit grid also turns the worksheet into a gentle health talk, and the tracing row builds the same pre-writing muscles the alphabet class uses.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy-habit awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing from life

What to say before you start: "This is a doctor — his tools help him take care of people. Trace his name, then find the three tools that belong with him. Now look at the six pictures: which ones show something healthy? Count the bottles slowly with your finger, and finish by drawing how YOU keep your body strong."

What to look for on the sheet: Point at the big picture together: the doctor wears a white coat and a blue tie and a stethoscope around his neck. In the match row, ask which tool would listen to a heartbeat. In the grid, ask your child to explain WHY a picture is or is not a healthy habit.

Questions to ask along the way: "Which doctor’s tool listens to your heart?" "Why do we wash hands before seeing the doctor?" "Which of the six habits do you do every day?" "What number did the medicine bottles count up to?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If a match line is hard, name the tools first and ask what each one touches. In the circle row, the tricky tiles are the ones that look fun — ask "does this help your body or just feel fun right now?" Count the bottles with one touch per bottle so the count stays honest.

Parent tips: Keep doctor talk friendly and honest — doctors help, and saying how you feel to a doctor is always allowed. Let your child own the pencil: the tracing can be wobbly and the drawing messy; the thinking is the work.

Understanding check: Ask: "Which tool listens to the heart? Name one healthy habit from the grid. How many bottles?" Right tool, one habit, the right count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Walk the healthy-habit grid at home today: the apple at snack time, the teeth brushing tonight, the running in the yard. Real repetition is what turns a circled picture into a habit.

Firefighter — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace FIRE FIGHTER, match the firefighter to the hose, helmet and fire truck, circle the tools a firefighter uses, count the fire helmets and draw stop-drop-and-roll.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a firefighter wears and carries, which tools fight fires, and the emergency move every child should own: stop, drop and roll.

Knowledge to have ready: Before starting, name the gear together: the helmet protects the head, the hose carries water, the truck rushes everything to the fire. Explain stop-drop-and-roll in one sentence — if clothes ever catch fire, we stop, drop to the ground, and roll until the fire is out.

Why this activity matters: Fire safety is a skill with real stakes, and rehearsal is what makes it stick. The tool grid sharpens "who uses what" thinking, the helmet count is gentle number practice, and the draw box lets your child rehearse the emergency move with their own hands.

  • Emergency vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Stop-drop-and-roll rehearsal
  • Counting to 7
  • Word tracing
  • Safety drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a firefighter. Trace the two words, then connect him to his hose, his helmet and his truck. Now look at the six tools — a firefighter carries some of them, but a couple belong to a mechanic or a student. Count the helmets with your finger, and then draw the safety move: stop, drop, and roll."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the yellow stripes on the firefighter’s coat and the badge on the helmet — real gear details to spot. In the grid, ask which tool sprays water and which one would fix a car instead. In the count row, helmets point in different directions; touch each one so none is counted twice.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the hose carry?" "Why does a firefighter wear a helmet?" "Which two tools in the grid are NOT for fighting fires?" "Show me stop, drop, and roll — can you do it on the carpet?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If the grid stalls, sort out loud: "sprays water, chops, lights the dark, puts out small fires — what’s left?" For the count, group the helmets into the top row and the bottom row first, then add the groups.

Parent tips: Practise stop-drop-and-roll for real on a carpet after the sheet — the body remembers what the pencil rehearses. Never make fire scary-for-fun: firefighters are helpers, and practicing the move is what keeps children safe.

Understanding check: Ask: "What do firefighters spray from the hose? Show me stop-drop-and-roll. How many helmets?" Water, the move, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Visit the drawing at bedtime: ask your child to SHOW the whole family how to stop, drop, and roll. Where is your family’s smoke alarm? Let your child find it — real maps of real safety.

Police Officer — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace POLICE OFFICER, match the officer to the badge, radio and patrol car, circle the things that keep people safe, count the traffic cones and draw a safe place to cross.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a police officer carries and drives, which objects help keep people safe, and what a safe street crossing looks like.

Knowledge to have ready: Officers are neighborhood helpers we can trust: the badge shows who they are, the radio calls for help, the patrol car takes them quickly to where they are needed. In any real worry, the plan is the same — find a grown-up you know, and officers are helpers too.

Why this activity matters: Safety tools become recognizable when children sort them on paper. The crossing draw-prompt opens the family conversation about how WE cross — a conversation worth having a hundred times before it is ever needed.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Safety-object awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Road-safety drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a police officer — a helper for the whole neighborhood. Trace the words, then connect the badge, the radio and the patrol car. Look at the six pictures: which ones help keep people safe? Count the cones carefully, then draw how WE cross the street safely."

What to look for on the sheet: Spot the gold badge on the cap and on the chest. In the grid, ask what each safety thing protects — a helmet protects heads, a cone warns cars, a first-aid kit helps hurts. In the draw box, ask for the stripes of the crosswalk before the pencil starts.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the badge tell us?" "Which grid pictures keep people safe, and how?" "Who holds your hand when we cross?" "What do the cones tell cars to do?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If the grid confuses, ask "does this protect a person or warn a car — or is it a toy?" The watch is the sneaky one: it tells time, but talk about whether it keeps someone SAFE. For the crossing drawing, stripes plus a grown-up’s hand are the key details.

Parent tips: Keep the message balanced — officers are helpers AND the first job in any worry is finding a grown-up you know. Practise the real crossing this week with the sheet’s words: stop, look, listen, hold hands.

Understanding check: Ask: "What does the radio do? Name two safety things from the grid. How do we cross the street?" Call-for-help, two objects, the family rule = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: On the next walk, find one real safety thing from the grid — a cone, a helmet rider, a crossing — and name it on the spot. Real streets make the worksheet real.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Who nurses are and what they carry, which daily habits keep bodies healthy, and caring-in-action — the worksheet’s last box asks your child to draw a nurse’s kindness.

Knowledge to have ready: Nurses take care of people beside doctors: the clipboard keeps notes, the bandage protects a scrape, the thermometer checks temperature. Nurses explain every step and have gentle hands — a friendly face at any check-up.

Why this activity matters: Meeting the nurse on paper makes real check-ups calmer, and the healthy-habit grid doubles as the family’s daily-health talk. The big bandage count is honest two-row counting practice with a purpose.

What to say before you start: "This is a nurse — she takes care of people with gentle hands. Trace her name, then connect her to the clipboard, the bandage and the thermometer. Now the five pictures: which are healthy habits? Count every bandage slowly — there are two rows — and draw how a nurse helps."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the cross on the clipboard and the stethoscope around the nurse’s neck. In the grid, ask why each circled habit helps the body. In the count, touch each bandage left to right, top row first — two rows of five make ten.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the thermometer check?" "Which habits did you circle, and when did you last do one?" "How many bandages in the top row? And the bottom?" "What would you want a nurse to say to you?"

Parent tips: If a real check-up is coming, this sheet is the warm-up: the nurse will explain first, and telling her how you feel is always allowed. Praise gentle hands during the drawing — kindness is the lesson under the lesson.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who takes care of people beside the doctor? Name one healthy habit you circled. How many bandages?" The team, one habit, ten = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Play nurse with a teddy tonight: wrap a toilet-paper bandage, check temperature with a hand on the forehead, explain every step out loud — exactly the worksheet, warm and alive.

Trace BAKER, match the baker to the bread, the mixing bowl and the oven mitt, circle the foods a baker can make, count the cupcakes and draw a treat you would like to bake.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a baker makes before the town wakes up, which tools bake bread and cakes, and which foods come from an oven — plus how to write the word BAKER.

Knowledge to have ready: A baker mixes, kneads and bakes: the mixing bowl holds the dough, the oven mitt protects hands from the hot oven, and bread, cookies, cakes and croissants all rise in the heat. Apples grow on trees — nobody bakes those!

Why this activity matters: Bakers turn simple flour into celebration food, and children know it in their bones. The baked-versus-grown sorting builds category thinking, and the treat-draw box opens the lovely family talk about which treats are worth baking together.

  • Kitchen vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Baked-versus-grown sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Treat drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a baker — she makes bread and treats while the town is still asleep. Trace her name, then connect the bread, the mixing bowl and the oven mitt. Now the six foods: which ones does the oven make? Count the cupcakes slowly, and then draw the treat YOU would bake."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the oven mitt and ask which hand it protects from what. In the grid, sort out loud: from the oven or off the tree? In the count row, cupcakes wait patiently — touch each swirl of frosting once and keep counting.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the baker pull out of the oven?" "Which foods in the grid did somebody bake?" "Why does the baker wear the big mitt?" "What would you bake first — and who would you share it with?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: One food in the grid has a stem and a shine — ask "does an oven grow this, or does an orchard?" The mitt is the clue to every other tile: oven-hot means baker-made. For the count, touch each cupcake swirl once.

Parent tips: Baking together is measuring, counting and patience in one delicious lesson — one batch of anything this week is enough. Let your child own the mixing and the pouring; the flour mess is the tuition.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who bakes our bread? Name two baked foods from the grid. How many cupcakes?" The baker, two bakes, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Bake one simple treat together this week — even a ready-mix counts. Let your child wear the mitt for real (empty-handed first!) and pull the tray out with you. The worksheet, but edible.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a barber does in the salon, which tools cut, dry and wash hair, and which tools belong to bathrooms and art boxes instead — plus how to write the word BARBER.

Knowledge to have ready: A barber cuts and shapes hair: the scissors snip, the comb straightens, the hairdryer blows warm air, and the shampoo bottle washes it all first. Hair keeps growing and growing, so the barber’s chair is a friend we visit again and again.

Why this activity matters: Haircut days go better when the tools are old friends on paper first. The tool grid sharpens bathroom-versus-salon-versus-art-box sorting, and the hairstyle draw box gives your child a say in their own look — small ownership, big cooperation.

  • Salon vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Hair-care sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Hairstyle drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a barber — the helper who keeps hair neat and tidy. Trace the name, then connect the scissors, the comb and the salon chair. Now the six pictures: which tools are for hair? Count the combs carefully, and then draw a hairstyle YOU think looks wonderful."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the big salon chair and ask what its lever does. In the grid, ask of each tool: hair, teeth, or paintings? The toothbrush and the paintbrush are visiting from other rooms. In the draw box, ask whether the hairstyle is for today or for a party.

Questions to ask along the way: "What do the scissors do in the salon?" "Which two grid tools are NOT for hair?" "What happens to hair when it grows?" "How do YOU like your hair — and who cuts it?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two tools in the grid look like close cousins of hair tools — one lives by the bathroom sink and one swims in a jar of paint water. Ask of each: does this snip, wash or style HAIR — or something else? For the count, combs lie in a row: one touch per tooth-holding tool.

Parent tips: If haircuts bring wiggles, this sheet is the warm-up: name the tools, let your child hold a comb during the real cut, and ask the barber to explain each step. Familiar tools make steady heads.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who cuts and styles hair? Name two hair tools from the grid. How many combs?" The barber, two tools, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Play salon tonight: a doll, a soft brush, a gentle mist of water, and your child as the barber explaining every step — snip, comb, dry. At the next real haircut, ask them to name the tools as they appear.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a construction worker builds and wears, which tools build walls and which build pictures, and why the hard hat and vest matter — plus how to write the words CONSTRUCTION WORKER.

Knowledge to have ready: Construction workers build the town: the hard hat protects the head, the safety vest makes the builder easy to see, and hammers, wrenches, saws and shovels do the heavy work. Pencils make the plans and paintbrushes add the color — at a desk, before and after the building!

Why this activity matters: Every crane and cone on the street becomes interesting once a child can name the world of work behind it. The tool grid sorts build-tools from desk-tools, and the hard hat opens the real site-safety talk: sites are for builders, and watchers stay outside the fence.

  • Building vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Work-tool sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Building drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a construction worker — the builder who makes houses, roads and towers. Trace the two long words, then connect the hard hat, the hammer and the safety vest. Now the six tools: which ones build things? Count the orange cones, and then draw a building YOU would love to make."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the yellow stripes on the safety vest and the shine on the hard hat. In the grid, ask of each tool: does this build, or does it write and paint? In the count row, cones often stand in a row like a little fence — count them with one touch each.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the hard hat protect?" "Which two tools in the grid work on paper, not on walls?" "What do the orange cones warn people about?" "What is YOUR building made of, and who lives in it?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two tools in the grid are desk friends — one makes plans and one makes pictures. Ask of each: would this hammer a nail, or help draw the house first? The saw, the shovel and the wrench are busy builders here.

Parent tips: Real building sites are exciting and dangerous — the rule for little watchers is simple: stay outside the fence with a grown-up, always. Point out hard hats and cones from the safe side of the street on your next walk instead.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who builds houses and towers? Name two building tools from the grid. How many cones?" The builder, two tools, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Walk past a real building site (from the safe side) and spot the grid together: hard hats, vests, cones, tools. Back home, build the drawn building from blocks — plans on paper first, exactly like real builders do.

Electrician — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace ELECTRICIAN, match the electrician to the light bulb, the wire and the tool belt, circle the things that use electricity, count the light bulbs and draw a safe way to use electricity.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What an electrician fixes and installs, which everyday things run on electricity, and the one big rule about sockets and wires — plus how to write the word ELECTRICIAN.

Knowledge to have ready: An electrician works with wires that carry electricity: the light bulb glows when the wires do their job, and the tool belt holds everything for safe repairs. Fans, washing machines, desk lamps and microwaves all drink electricity — bicycles and soccer balls run on legs instead!

Why this activity matters: Electricity is invisible, so naming what it powers makes it thinkable — and the safety rule becomes real: never poke sockets, never touch wires, and keep water far from plugs. That rule, learned young, is a lifelong shield.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Electricity awareness
  • Electric-safety rules
  • Word tracing
  • Safety drawing

What to say before you start: "This is an electrician — the helper who takes care of the wires that bring us light. Trace the long word, then connect the light bulb, the wire and the tool belt. Now the six pictures: which ones need electricity to work? Count the bulbs, and then draw one safe way WE use electricity at home."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the tool belt and ask what a repair helper carries in it. In the grid, ask of each tile: plug in, or leg power? In the draw box, praise any picture where a grown-up’s hands do the plugging — that is the safety rule drawn in crayon.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the electrician fix?" "Which grid things drink electricity?" "What runs your bicycle instead?" "What is our family rule about sockets and wires?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two tiles in the grid are powered by you — pedals and kicks. Ask of each: does this need a plug, or strong muscles? And the big rule hides in every home: sockets and wires are grown-ups’ business only.

Parent tips: Say the rule until it is furniture: never poke sockets, never chew or touch cords, keep water far from plugs — and always tell a grown-up about sparks or frayed wires. Calm repetition, not fear, is what keeps children safe.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who fixes the wires? Name two things that use electricity. What do we never poke?" The electrician, two plugs, sockets = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Do a socket safari at home today: find every outlet, every cord and every plug — count them, name what each powers, and practise the rule with your hands behind your back. Real house, real rule, real safety.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a plumber fixes behind walls and under sinks, which tools steer the water, and why water is worth saving — plus how to write the word PLUMBER.

Knowledge to have ready: A plumber takes care of the pipes that bring clean water in and carry used water out: the pipe wrench turns big pipe nuts, the plunger politely pushes a blockage away, and the toolbox holds it all. Water is precious — turning the tap off while brushing is a plumber’s favorite trick.

Why this activity matters: Plumbers are invisible helpers until a pipe bursts, and this sheet makes them visible and valued. The tool grid invites careful talk about each tool, and the save-water draw box plants an earth-caring habit that pays for itself on the next bill.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Water awareness
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Water-saving drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a plumber — the helper who takes care of our water pipes. Trace the name, then connect the pipe wrench, the toolbox and the sink. Now the six tools: which ones does a plumber really use? Let’s talk about each. Count the pipes, and then draw one way to save water at home."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the sink in the match row and trace where the water goes. In the grid, take each tool one at a time — the hammer builds, the paintbrush paints, and the wrenches and the plunger work with water. In the pipe drawing, pipes bend and cross; follow each one with a finger so the count stays true.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the pipe wrench turn?" "Which two grid tools belong to a builder and an artist instead?" "Where does the water go when it leaves our sink?" "How can WE save water today?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two tools in the grid never touch a pipe — one bangs nails and one swims in paint. Ask of each tool: does this help water flow, or does it do a different job altogether?

Parent tips: Turn the tap off while brushing teeth — two minutes, twice a day, a small bucket saved every single time. If a plumber ever visits, let your child watch the wrench work and hand over the flashlight: helpers love small apprentices.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who fixes the pipes? Name two plumber tools from the grid. How can we save water?" The plumber, two tools, one saving idea = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Tonight, brush teeth with the tap OFF and count the seconds together — then celebrate the saved water out loud. Small ritual, real habit, exactly what the draw box was for.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a mechanic fixes under the hood, which tools mend engines, and how to tell a mechanic’s tools from a doctor’s — plus how to write the word MECHANIC.

Knowledge to have ready: A mechanic keeps cars and trucks running: the wrench turns the bolts, the toolbox holds every size, and the car rolls up on its tires for a check. Here is a funny one — a stethoscope listens to hearts, not engines; that tool belongs to the doctor!

Why this activity matters: The mechanic-versus-doctor mix-up is the funniest, most memorable sort on the whole set — and memorable is the point. Naming the garage world makes every oil stop interesting, and the vehicle draw box turns observers into little engineers.

What to say before you start: "This is a mechanic — the helper who keeps cars running strong. Trace the name, then connect the wrench, the toolbox and the car. Now the six tools: which ones fix engines? One of them is very silly here! Count the tires on the red car, and then draw the vehicle YOU would love to fix."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the red car in the match row and count its wheels right on the sheet. In the grid, ask of each tool: would this fix an engine, a wooden shelf, or a person? The stethoscope is the giggler — it listens to people, not pickups. In the draw box, ask for a hood that really opens.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the mechanic turn with the wrench?" "Which grid tool belongs to the doctor, and why is that funny?" "What do tires do for a car?" "What vehicle would YOU fix first — and what is broken on it?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: One tool in the grid is wearing the wrong uniform — ask "who listens with this, a mechanic or a doctor?" For every other tool, wonder out loud: would this turn a bolt, cut wood, or fix something else entirely?

Parent tips: Next oil change or tire stop, bring the vocabulary: let your child name the wrench, the jack, the tires. Garages are workplaces, not playgrounds — watching happens beside a grown-up, always.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who fixes cars? Name two mechanic tools from the grid. How many tires does the red car have?" The mechanic, two tools, the tire count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Bicycle maintenance day: pump the tires, check the brakes, wipe the frame — with your child as head mechanic explaining each move. Two wheels are the perfect first garage.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a pilot does in the cockpit, which papers and maps fly along, and which things belong aboard an airplane — plus how to write the word PILOT.

Knowledge to have ready: The pilot flies the airplane and keeps every passenger safe: the passport shows who you are in other countries, the flight map shows the way through the sky, and aboard the plane the seat belt clicks for takeoff and landing. Headphones, suitcases and life vests fly along too.

Why this activity matters: First flights are big feelings in small bodies. Naming the pilot, the papers and the plane’s things turns the airport from chaos into a checklist your child can own — and the seat-belt rule rehearsed here rides along on every trip.

  • Airport vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Air-travel sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Journey drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a pilot — the captain who flies the airplane. Trace the name, then connect the airplane, the passport and the flight map. Now the six pictures: which ones belong on a plane? Count the airplanes carefully, and then draw a safe trip through the sky — seat belt on!"

What to look for on the sheet: Find the wings on the airplane and the lines on the flight map. In the grid, ask of each tile: does this fly with us, or does it stay home? The sandwich starts a good conversation about snacks and suitcases. In the draw box, ask for the seat belt across the little traveler’s lap.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the passport tell people?" "What does the seat belt do for takeoff?" "Which grid things ride along in a suitcase?" "Where would YOU fly, and who would you visit?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: One tile in the grid is round, bouncy and better off in the park. The little sandwich is a friendly question — ask "is a snack part of the airplane, or part of your carry-on?" There is room to talk about both. For the count, planes point different ways: touch each one once.

Parent tips: Flying soon? Rehearse the sequence on the sheet: buckle the seat belt low and tight, stay seated when the seat-belt sign is on, and listen to the crew — they are the captain’s helpers. Calm practice beats airport panic, every time.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who flies the airplane? Name two things that belong aboard. What do we do for takeoff?" The pilot, two things, buckle up = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Flying this year? Let your child carry their own small backpack and click their own seat belt — then point out the real flight map on the seat-back screen. The sheet, but at 30,000 feet.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a flight attendant does for passengers, the four rules of flying safely, and which rules are safe and which are not — plus how to write the words FLIGHT ATTENDANT.

Knowledge to have ready: The flight attendant takes care of everyone aboard: the tray carries meals and drinks down the aisle, the seat belt keeps every body snug for takeoff and landing, and the crew’s gentle voice is the one to listen to. Aisles are for walking only — and never during takeoff!

Why this activity matters: The cabin crew are the sky’s crossing guards: their rules keep a whole plane of wiggly travelers safe. Sorting the safe rules from the silly one lets your child rehearse the real flight before it happens — and giving the rules a face makes them easy to follow.

  • Airport vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Flying-safety rules
  • Safe-versus-unsafe sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Seat drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a flight attendant — she takes care of everyone on the airplane. Trace the two words, then connect the tray, the seat belt and the airplane. Now the four rules: which are safe? Count the suitcases slowly, and then draw you in a safe seat, belt clicked and ready to fly."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the tray and ask what travels on it — juice, meals, and sometimes a smile. In the grid, read each rule aloud and act the safe ones out: hands click an imaginary belt, bottoms sit tall. Let your child catch the aisle-run rule with a big NO.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the flight attendant carry on the tray?" "Which three rules are safe?" "Why do we stay seated for takeoff and landing?" "What does the seat belt sound like when it clicks?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Three rules keep every flyer snug and one rule would tumble a tray — the unsafe one happens in the aisle. Read all four out loud: safe rules sound steady, and the silly one sounds fast.

Parent tips: On your next flight, introduce your child to a crew member and let them show off the belt — the crew are the rules’ own grown-ups, and children follow a face better than a lecture. Trash in the bin, tray folded: the whole sheet, lived.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who takes care of passengers in the sky? Name two safe flying rules. Is running in the aisle safe or unsafe?" The crew, two rules, unsafe = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Rehearse with a kitchen chair: sit tall, click an imaginary belt, fold the tray, ask to move — grown-up style. Then fly it to the living room. The whole sheet, landed softly on the carpet.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a train conductor does aboard the cars, the four rules of riding trains safely, and which rules are safe and which are not — plus how to write the words TRAIN CONDUCTOR.

Knowledge to have ready: The conductor checks tickets, calls the stations and keeps every rider on course: the ticket is your pass to ride, the whistle wakes the train, and the yellow line on the platform is the place where waiting feet stop. Windows are for looking — never for leaning!

Why this activity matters: Trains are magical AND heavy, which is exactly why the yellow line matters. Sorting safe from unsafe rules gives your child the platform talk before the platform does — and the somewhere-new draw box turns rail safety into adventure planning.

What to say before you start: "This is the train conductor — the captain of the whole train. Trace the two words, then connect the train, the ticket and the whistle. Now the four rules: which are safe? Count the windows on the long train, and then draw where YOUR train would go — somewhere brand new!"

What to look for on the sheet: Find the engine at the front of the long train and count the cars it pulls. In the grid, read each rule aloud — sitting bottoms, staying close to your adult, waiting feet behind the yellow line — and let your child veto the window-lean with a strong NO.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the conductor do with the ticket?" "Which three train rules are safe?" "Why do we stand behind the yellow line?" "Where would YOUR train go first?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Three rules keep every rider on track and one tips people out the window — the wobbly one is about leaning. Read all four with wide-open ears; the safe ones stand still and the unsafe one stretches.

Parent tips: On a real platform, the ritual is: hand in hand, back from the yellow line, and never near the edge while the train arrives. Say it the same way every time — sameness is what makes the rule stick when the whistle blows.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who is the captain of the train? Name two safe train rules. Where do waiting feet stop?" The conductor, two rules, the yellow line = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Ride a real train, a tram or the airport shuttle this month and rehearse the sheet: ticket checked, yellow line respected, window admired with eyes only. The somewhere-new box comes true the moment the wheels start.

What to look for on the sheet: Find the scanner and ask what the beep means — it reads the price! In the grid, name each thing and ask which basket it belongs in: food, toys, or school supplies. In the count row, apples like to huddle: count from one end to the other, one gentle touch each.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the scanner beep for?" "What does the receipt tell us?" "Which of the six things would YOU put in the basket first?" "What does the cashier say when we pay?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: This grid is the generous kind — every single tile belongs at the store, so circle proudly and name what each one is for. For the count, work from one end of the apples to the other so none rolls out of the count.

Parent tips: At the real checkout, hand over the sheet’s jobs: your child places the basket items on the belt, watches the scanner beep and holds the receipt. Money talk can wait — the sequence is the lesson.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who takes our money at the store? Name two things you can buy there. What does the receipt do?" The cashier, two buys, the story-on-paper = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Play store tonight with the pantry and a shoebox till: your child is the cashier, you are the customer, and the receipt is scribbled on paper. Real script, real beeps, whole worksheet alive.

Knowledge to have ready: An animal shelter is a safe waiting place for animals without homes: the kennel is each dog’s own room, the food bowl fills every day, and the worker feeds, brushes, walks and loves every animal until a family comes. Every one of the six caring ways on the sheet is right.

Why this activity matters: This is the empathy sheet of the set: every tile is a kind act, so the circle step becomes a chorus of yeses. Drawing an animal that needs a home gives big feelings a safe place to land — and plants the family conversation about how we help real animals.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who cares for animals at the shelter? Name two ways to care for an animal. Which one will YOU do today?" The worker, two ways, one today = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Do one caring act from the grid for a real or stuffed animal tonight — brush, feed, pet, play, a warm bath or extra love. Then ask your child which way was easiest and which was hardest. Kindness grows by doing.

What the child is learning: What a lifeguard watches for at the pool, the safe swimming rules on the sheet — and the two unsafe ones to catch — plus how to write the word LIFEGUARD.

Knowledge to have ready: A lifeguard sits high where the whole pool is in view, with a whistle for warnings and a rescue float for saving. The safe rules on this sheet: swim with a grown-up and walk on the pool deck. The tricky two? Running near the pool and diving in the shallow end — the red cross and green check marks have opinions about all four!

Why this activity matters: Water is the most serious safety topic in this whole collection, and four-year-olds are exactly the right age to start the rules. The check-and-cross marks let your child judge each rule out loud — sorting safe from unsafe is the core skill of every pool summer to come.

  • Pool-safety rules

What to say before you start: "This is a lifeguard — the helper who watches over everyone in the water. Trace the name, then connect the whistle, the rescue float and the pool. Now the four rules: which are safe? The green checks and red crosses have opinions! Count the beach balls, and then draw YOU being safe near water."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the rescue float and ask who it is for — a tired swimmer, held out long before any trouble. In the grid, read each rule aloud and ask your child to judge it before peeking at the marks: is running safe on a wet, slippery deck? In the draw box, walking feet matter most.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the lifeguard’s whistle mean?" "Which two rules are safe, and what makes them safe?" "Why do we walk near the pool?" "Who is YOUR grown-up in the water, every single time?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two rules keep swimmers safe and two are sneaky — the fast ones. Ask of each rule: would the lifeguard’s whistle blow at this? The green check means safe and the red cross means never; listen to both.

Parent tips: The non-negotiables, said warmly and often: never swim without a grown-up, walk on the deck, and ask before going near ANY water — pools, buckets, ponds. Practise the walking feet on a real deck edge this summer; legs remember what pencils rehearse.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who watches the pool? Name one safe rule and one unsafe rule you caught. What does the red cross mean?" The lifeguard, the rules, no-never = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: At the next pool or bath, rehearse the sheet: grown-up first, walking feet, ask permission. Give your child the job of spotting the real lifeguard at every pool you visit — the watcher of the water, found in real life.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who plays music for a living? Name two instruments from the grid. What does the microphone really do?" The musician, two instruments, makes-it-louder = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Have a kitchen-band concert tonight: one pot drummer, one shaker in a bottle, one singer with a pretend microphone — the grid, brought to life at full volume. Curtain call at bedtime.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the garbage truck do on our street?" "Which four things go in the recycling bin?" "Where does the banana peel go instead — and what does it become?" "What do the safety gloves do?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two items in the grid are not for the recycling bin — one is shiny and crinkly, and one used to be fruit. Ask of each: recycle bin, compost pile, or trash can? The garden would love one of them.

Parent tips: Trucks and bins are work zones: keep little watchers well back on collection day — never behind a reversing truck, never inside a bin. Then sort tonight’s recycling together and let your child be the checker: bottle, box, can, jar — the sheet, done for real.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who keeps our town clean? Name two things that can be recycled. Where does the banana peel go?" The worker, two recyclables, the compost = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Start a small compost jar or corner this week for peels and apple cores — let your child feed it daily and watch it change. The grid’s trickiest tile becomes a living science experiment on the windowsill.

COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

School Counselor — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace COUNSELOR, match the counselor to the school, the speech bubble and the helping hand, circle the kind ways to help a friend, count the conversation cards and draw someone you can talk to.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Who the school counselor is and how they help, four kind ways to help a friend — and the two unkind ones to catch — plus how to write the word COUNSELOR.

Knowledge to have ready: A school counselor is a feelings helper: the speech bubble means listening and talking, the helping hand means steady support, and their door is open when a day feels too big. Kind friends listen, help, share and are kind — laughing AT someone and ignoring someone are the two tricks to catch.

Why this activity matters: This is the heart sheet of the set: every tile is either a kindness or a trap, and four-year-olds are at exactly the age when friendship habits set. Sorting kind from unkind gives your child the words for the playground, and the draw box names a real person to talk to — a safety net drawn in crayon.

  • Feelings vocabulary
  • Kind-versus-unkind sorting
  • Helper awareness
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Trusted-adult drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a school counselor — a helper for feelings and friendships. Trace the name, then connect the school, the speech bubble and the helping hand. Now the six ways to treat a friend: which ones are kind? Two are tricks! Count the conversation cards, and then draw YOUR person to talk to when a day feels big."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the speech bubble and ask what it is full of — words worth listening to. In the grid, read each way aloud and ask your child to make a kind face or a no-thank-you face at each one. Laughing AT someone and ignoring someone get the biggest no faces of all.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the school counselor do all day?" "Which four ways are kind to a friend?" "What could you say if a friend feels sad?" "Who is YOUR talk-to person — and what would you tell them?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Kind ways make friends feel bigger; the tricky ones make friends feel small. Ask of each tile: would I like it if someone did this to ME? That one question sorts the whole grid.

Parent tips: Teach the golden test as a daily habit — would I like that done to me? — and let your child hear you use it too. The draw box matters most here: name the real people your child can always talk to, at school and at home, and say it out loud together.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who is the feelings helper at school? Name two kind ways to treat a friend. Which two ways are not kind?" The counselor, two kindnesses, the two tricks = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Practise one circled kindness today — listen to a sibling’s whole story, share a snack, help set the table. Then ask your child to name their talk-to people while pointing at the drawing. Safety nets work best when they are spoken out loud.

COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Scientist — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace SCIENTIST, match the scientist to the microscope, the beaker and the safety goggles, circle the things used in a science lab, count the test tubes and draw something you would like to discover.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a scientist does in the lab, which tools hold, magnify and protect, and which grid tiles belong to the kitchen, the library and the craft box — plus how to write the word SCIENTIST.

Knowledge to have ready: A scientist asks questions and tests them: the microscope makes tiny things huge, the beaker holds liquids for mixing, and the safety goggles protect curious eyes. Test tubes, flasks and magnifying glasses live in the lab — apples live in kitchens, books in libraries, scissors in craft boxes!

Why this activity matters: The lab is where curiosity becomes a job, and this sheet hands your child the tools to imagine it. Tile-by-tile sorting builds the careful looking real science runs on, and the discover-draw box ends the whole collection with the biggest question of all: what will YOU find out?

  • Science vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Lab sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Discovery drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a scientist — the helper who asks questions and finds answers. Trace the name, then connect the microscope, the beaker and the safety goggles. Now the six pictures: which ones really work in a lab? Let’s talk about each one. Count the test tubes in the rack, and then draw something YOU would love to discover."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the goggles and ask what they protect — a scientist’s eyes come first! In the grid, go tile by tile and ask where each thing really lives: the lab, the kitchen, the library or the craft drawer. In the count row, test tubes stand in a rack like crayons in a box — count left to right, one touch each.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the microscope make bigger?" "Why does a scientist wear goggles?" "Which grid tiles belong to other rooms — and which rooms?" "What would YOU love to discover one day?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Take each tile to its home: the lab, the fruit bowl, the bookshelf or the craft table — ask of each: would this sit on a lab bench, or somewhere else altogether? The goggles-and-gloves scientist only uses what belongs in the lab.

Parent tips: Labs have one big rule worth borrowing at home: real experiments happen WITH a grown-up and safety first. Do a kitchen-lab session — baking soda, vinegar, goggles from the dress-up box — and let your child narrate like the scientist they drew.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who asks questions for a living? Name two lab tools from the grid. What do the goggles protect?" The scientist, two tools, the eyes = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Do one tiny experiment this week — sink or float, baking-soda fizz, a magnifying glass over a leaf. Ask first, guess second, watch third: that order IS science, and your child just did it.
